Nutrient exchange of extensive cyanobacterial mats in an arid subtropical wetland

Maria Fernanda AdameA,B,D, Ruth ReefA, Alistair GrinhamC, Glen HolmesA and Catherine E. LovelockA

ASchool of Biological Sciences, The University of Queensland, St Lucia, Qld 4072, Australia.
BCentro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del Instituto Politécnico Nacional (CINVESTAV), Unidad Mérida, 97310, Yucatán, México.
CSchool of Engineering, The University of Queensland, St Lucia, Qld 4072, Australia.
DCorresponding author. Email: mfadame@mda.cinvestav.mx

Abstract. Cyanobacterial mats cover extensive areas of subtropical arid coastal wetlands and are sites of active nutrient exchange. To assess spatial (low v. high in the intertidal zone) and temporal (day v. night) variability in nitrogen (N) exchange in arid Exmouth Gulf, Western Australia, we measured nutrient exchange (NO\(_x^-\)-N, NH\(_4^+\) and soluble reactive phosphorus) during tidal inundation and N fixation of cyanobacterial mats before and during an unusual period of heavy rainfall. Additionally, we investigated the species composition within the cyanobacterial mat. We hypothesised that nutrients are released to the floodwater during tidal inundation, that N fixation is a significant path of N incorporation, that highest N fixation rates occur in the low intertidal zone at night, and that the cyanobacterial mat community composition varies across the intertidal zone. Our results showed that nutrients were removed from the floodwater during tidal inundation. N fixation accounted for 34% of N incorporation, with highest rates in the lower intertidal zone during the day. The cyanobacterial mat was dominated by Microcoleus chthonoplastes, but composition varied across the intertidal zone. The present study provided evidence of temporal and spatial variability in nutrient exchange and implied an important role of cyanobacterial mats in coastal production.

Additional keywords: Exmouth Gulf, Giralia Bay, nitrogen fixation, phosphorus, tidal exchange.

Received 11 June 2011, accepted 29 February 2012, published online 4 May 2012

Introduction
Coastal tropical wetlands are composed of a range of communities of primary producers that inhabit the intertidal zone where they are periodically flooded by tides. These communities are often distributed as distinct strips of vegetation types arranged in parallel zones along an elevation gradient. Mangroves usually grow at low elevations, where they are frequently flooded by tides. Saltmarsh and cyanobacterial mats occupy higher elevations, where tidal flooding is less frequent. Conditions in the high intertidal zone are extremely harsh, with long periods of desiccation and high levels of temperature and salinity. In subtropical arid regions, where temperatures are high and salinity can reach extremely high values (>90), cyanobacterial mats are the most competitive community in the high intertidal zone, where they occupy extensive areas (Paling and McComb 1994; Whitton and Potts 2000).

Cyanobacterial mats are highly productive communities of cyanobacteria, bacteria, archea, diatoms and other microorganisms capable of tolerating the extreme environmental conditions found in the intertidal zone (Potts 1999; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). They are an essential component of the nutrient cycling along the coast, where they stabilise sediment and provide food for a range of marine and terrestrial animals (Pulich and Scalan 1987; Paterson et al. 1990; Paling and McComb 1994). Cyanobacterial mats occur in a wide range of ecosystems characterised by extreme environmental fluctuations, including hypersaline lakes, thermal springs, Antarctic lakes, deserts and intertidal sediments (Stal 1995). Although cyanobacterial mats have been widely studied in many locations, especially in temperate regions, the role of cyanobacterial mats in coastal production of subtropical arid regions is poorly understood.

Cyanobacterial mats can fix significant amounts of N in coastal wetlands (Paling and McComb 1994; Lee and Joye 2006). This fixed N, together with other nutrients and carbohydrates, may be leached from the cyanobacterial mat during tidal inundation and transported to adjacent mangrove forests and estuaries, where it may provide nutrient subsidies to the coastal zone (Paling and McComb 1994; Lovelock et al. 2010). In oligotrophic areas, the subsidies from the cyanobacterial mat could be especially important in sustaining coastal production (McKinnon and Ayukai 1996).

The biogeochemical function of cyanobacterial mats is complex and variable among regions, seasons and different

environmental conditions (Toledo et al. 1995; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). Thus, it is important to understand the function of this intertidal ecosystem at a regional scale, particularly because of its potential importance to nutrient cycling and coastal foodwebs, including fisheries (McKinnon and Ayukai 1996). Furthermore, the study of the environmental function of cyanobacterial mats can provide valuable information on life forms in extreme environments, the origin of life on earth and extraterrestrial life (Paerl et al. 2000; Rothschild and Mancinelli 2001).

The main objective of the present study was to increase our understanding of nutrient exchange in cyanobacterial mats of subtropical arid regions and their potential role in subsiding coastal production. To do this, we focussed on N fixation and nutrient exchange during tidal inundation, because these processes are important mechanisms of exchange between the cyanobacterial mat, the atmosphere and the coastal ocean. Additionally, we aimed to identify the cyanobacteria of the mat by using both morphological observations and genetic identification.

The study was conducted in Exmouth Gulf in Western Australia, a subtropical arid embayment surrounded by extensive cyanobacterial mats (Brunskill et al. 2001). Exmouth Gulf is an oligotrophic embayment, yet it supports a highly productive fishery and is one of the last pristine arid estuaries in the world (Sporer et al. 2005). In the present study, we tested the following hypotheses: H1 – dissolved nutrients are released from the cyanobacterial mat to the floodwater during tidal inundation; H2 – nutrient exchange is higher in the day than at night; H3 – N fixation is a significant component of N incorporation into the cyanobacterial mat; H4 – N fixation rates are higher during night than day; H5 – N fixation is higher in the low than in the high intertidal zone; and H6 – species composition within the cyanobacterial mat is variable across the intertidal zone.

Materials and methods
Site description
Exmouth Gulf is an estuarine embayment on the western coast of Australia. The Gulf is an inverse mesotidal estuary (tidal range of 1.6 m) with very limited riverine inputs (Brunskill et al. 2001). The area is arid, with an annual rainfall of only 300 mm, compared with 2500 mm of evaporation (Lough 1998). The Gulf is surrounded by a narrow fringe of mangroves (116 km²) and extensive salt flats (1026 km²) at higher elevations partly covered with carpet-like cyanobacterial mats (>100 km²) (Brunskill et al. 2001). The monthly mean minimum and maximum temperatures are 24°C in the winter and 38°C in the summer, but the temperature can reach 49°C (1975–2011, Australian Bureau of Meteorology; Learmonth airport station; http://www.bom.gov.au/, accessed February 2010). The area receives frequent cyclones which deliver strong pulses of freshwater and nutrients to the Gulf, affecting primary and secondary production (McKinnon et al. 2003; Lovelock et al. 2011). Exmouth Gulf supports one of the most important prawn fisheries in Australia (Sporer et al. 2005).

The site for the present study was at Giralia Bay (22°26′13″S, 114°20′46″E) on the eastern side of Sandalwood Peninsula on the edge of a tidal creek (Fig. 1). At this site, the cyanobacterial mat occupies a wide area between 230 and 270 cm above the lowest astronomical tide (Lovelock et al. 2010). Experiments were performed in March 2008. During this time, a tropical cyclone (Cyclone Pancho) approached the coast, resulting in storm-like conditions, with unusually high rainfall (263 mm in 4 days, Australian Bureau of Meteorology, http://www.bom.gov.au/, accessed February 2010). During the field experiments, water temperature and light intensity decreased as Cyclone Pancho approached the coast causing cloudy skies, heavy rainfall and strong winds. To monitor the variations in light and temperature as a result of the approaching cyclone, water

temperature and surface photosynthetically active radiation were logged in situ during our field experiments. Temperature loggers (HOBO Pendant Data Logger, ONSET Computer Corporation, Pocasset, MA, USA) were fixed just above the mat surface and logged temperature at 10-min intervals. Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) loggers (Odyssey, Dataflow Systems, Christchurch, New Zealand) were fixed adjacent to the benthic mat, with a logging rate of 10 min. During the first day of sampling, the midday water temperature was ~32°C; by the end of the week, it had dropped to ~22°C. Surface PAR peaked at ~2000 μmol quanta m^{-2} s^{-1} during the first day of sampling and dropped more than 50%, to ~900 μmol quanta m^{-2} s^{-1} by the end of the week.

We conducted field and laboratory experiments addressing two major functions of the cyanobacterial mat in the intertidal zone, namely, nutrient exchange during tidal inundation and N fixation. Additionally, we collected samples of cyanobacterial mat to examine its species composition.

Nutrient exchange

Nutrient exchange during tidal inundation

To test our first two hypotheses, we measured nutrient exchange between the cyanobacterial mat and the floodwater. We followed two approaches, including (1) field sampling during tidal inundation as floodwater moved in and out of the cyanobacterial mat and (2) experiments of nutrient exchange in chambers.

In the field, we measured nutrient exchange during three spring tidal cycles (24, 26 and 27 March 2008) with 2.58-, 2.59- and 2.50-m amplitude, respectively. Tides were sampled from the beginning of the flood to the end of the ebb tide from 1200 hours to 1730 hours, 1300 hours to 1650 hours, and 1400 hours to 1745 hours, respectively. A sample of water was taken at three points in the mid-intertidal zone of the cyanobacterial mat (Fig. 1). The first samples were taken as soon as the mat was flooded and the water height reached 10 cm. From that point, the sites were sampled every hour at 10 cm above the mat, through high tide (water height of ~40–50 cm), and until the end of the ebb tide, when the water leaving the cyanobacterial mat was 10 cm deep. Although there are limitations of using this sampling technique (e.g. lateral flow of the tide, absence of ‘control’ samples that were not in contact with the cyanobacterial mat), the data collected in the field allowed us to compare the nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat in situ with nutrient exchange in controlled experiments in the chambers. During collection, samples were filtered through a 0.45-μm MF filter (Millipex-HA, Millipore, MA, USA), stored in 20-mL acid-washed (10% HCl) high-density polyethylene scintillation vials, and kept frozen until analysis. Samples were analysed within 2 weeks of collection. Ammonium (NH_4^+-N) was analysed by the fluorescence method (Holmes et al. 1999), and nitrogen oxides (NO_3^-N + NO_2^-N = NO_x^-N) and soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) were measured using colourimetric analysis with a nutrient analyser AQ-2 SEAL (AI Scientific, Scarborough, QLD, Australia).

Nutrient exchange in chambers

Nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat with the overlying water was compared in chambers between (1) cyanobacterial mat and sediment without cyanobacterial mat in the light, (2) cyanobacterial mat and sediment without cyanobacterial mat in the dark and (3) desiccated and wet cyanobacterial mat.

The samples were collected from the mid-intertidal zone at low tide by pushing a specially manufactured ‘chamber’ of transparent polycarbonate cylinder of 5-cm diameter into the substrate and carefully lifting it with the cyanobacterial mat (~1 cm thick) and the underlying sediment (~3 cm thick). The chambers with the cyanobacterial mats were transported to Giralia Station homestead where the experiments were conducted within the next 12 h. The chambers were filled with 200 mL of 0.22 μm-filtered seawater (MF Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) collected from the site. Because of variable conditions over the days, seawater nutrient concentrations used during incubations varied slightly among experimental runs. The chambers were left uncovered to allow for gas exchange with the atmosphere. To simulate night conditions, chambers were covered with aluminium foil, but the experiments were run during the day. Therefore, we will refer to the results as ‘light’ and ‘dark’ experiments, in contrast to N-fixation experiments, which were run during day and night (thus ‘day’ and ‘night’ experiments). Overlying water was stirred using magnetic stirrers. Initial samples were taken as soon as the water was poured into all the chambers and then every 2 h for 6–8 h. The samples were taken at 3 cm above the cyanobacterial mat with a syringe and a plastic hose. Samples were filtered, preserved and analysed as described above for field experiments. For the third experiment, where wet cyanobacterial mat was compared with desiccated mat, half of the cyanobacterial-mat samples were dried in air under a light intensity of 120 μmol quanta m^{-2} s^{-1} (within the range of conditions to those of our field experiments in the morning on a cloudy day) and the other half was kept wet in the aquarium.

Nitrogen fixation

To test our third, fourth and fifth hypotheses, we conducted the following two experiments: (1) N fixation during the day v. night, using six samples of cyanobacterial mat collected from the mid-intertidal zone; and (2) N fixation in low v. high intertidal zone, using three samples collected from each zone (Fig. 1).

The cyanobacterial mat and sediment without cyanobacterial mat were collected in the same way as for the nutrient-exchange experiments (see above). N fixation was determined using the acetylene to ethylene reduction method (Hardy et al. 1968). Acetylene gas was generated in the field from the reaction of calcium carbide with deionised water. A sample of the generated acetylene gas was kept from each experiment to test for ethylene contamination. Before each experiment, the chambers were filled with 120 mL of 0.22 μm-filtered seawater (MF Millipore) collected from the site, and 30 mL of filtered seawater saturated with acetylene. The chamber base was adjusted such that the headspace within the chamber was 30 mL. The lids of the chambers were sealed with gas-tight septa, through which two needles were placed. The first needle was a long 75-mm 18G needle fitted with a Luer-lok 3-way stopcock (Dickinson and Company, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) to allow gas injections into the liquid phase. The second needle was a double-ended Vacutainer needle (Dickinson and Company) for the collection of headspace gas samples. Throughout the experiment, the water in

<page number="3">

the chamber was kept in constant motion by using a magnetic stirrer. For each experiment, a blank sample of filtered seawater was also incorporated.

At the beginning of the experiment, 10 mL of acetylene gas was injected into the liquid phase, displacing 10 mL of headspace gas. Headspace samples were collected at intervals of 2 h for 6 h. Samples of the headspace gas were collected using 5-mL glass Vacutainers while simultaneously injecting 5 mL of acetylene gas into the liquid phase of the chamber to maintain acetylene concentrations within the chamber. Experiments testing N fixation were run during the day and night. In experiments testing N fixation during the day, the chambers were placed in direct sunlight inside a container filled with cool water to maintain a constant chamber temperature (25°C). Both light and temperature levels were monitored while the chambers were running. Levels of PAR were recorded using a Li-Cor light meter data logger (L1-1400, LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA).

Headspace gas samples were analysed for ethylene in a gas chromatograph (6890 GC System with FID, Hewlett-Packard, Palo Alto, CA) fitted with a GS-Gas Pro PLOT column (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). The concentration of ethylene was determined via the procedure outlined in Davey et al. (2008). N fixation was expressed as moles of ethylene and as N fixed using the ratio of three moles of ethylene to one mole of N, the ratio of conversion recommended for cyanobacteria (Howarth et al. 1988).

Cyanobacterial mat composition
To identify the main species comprising the cyanobacterial mat and to determine the variability across the intertidal zone (H6), we used morphological observations and molecular techniques. We collected five 40 cm × 40 cm squares of ~2-cm depth of cyanobacterial mat. The samples were collected from the low and high intertidal zones (Fig. 1). The mat was transported dry to the laboratory where subsamples were rehydrated in seawater and inspected under a dissecting microscope (Nikon 15Z, Nikon, Tokyo, Japan). Morphotypes were picked from the samples and mounted on glass slides for examination at ×1000 magnification. Identification to genus was made according to Drouet (1981).

The cyanobacterial mat collected for the visual inspection was also used for the 16s rDNA sequencing. Genomic DNA was extracted from the top 5 mm of eight cores of mat (3 cm²) from the low and high intertidal zones, using a modification of the method of Nubel et al. (1997). Samples were homogenised in 1 mL of 1 M NaCl by using a Tissue Tearor (BioSpec Products Inc., Bartlesville, OK, USA). Cyanobacteria were lysed by three freeze–thaw cycles (in liquid N₂), followed by incubation for 20 min at 50°C in 5 mL of TESC buffer (100 mM pH 8.0 TRIS–HCl, 1.5 M NaCl, 100 mM EDTA, 1% CTAB, 100 μg mL⁻¹ proteinase K, and 1% SDS). The DNA was extracted from the homogenate by using a phenol–chloroform–isoamyl alcohol extraction. Cyanobacteria 16S rDNA was amplified from the cyanobacteria DNA by using the CYA359F (GGGGAATYTTCCGCAATGGG) and CYA781R (an equimolar mix of GACTACTGGGGTATCTAATCCATT and GACTACAGGGGTATCTAATCCCTTT) primers from Nubel et al. (1997). A 40-nucleotide GC clamp (CGCCCGCCGCG CCCCGCGCCGGTCCCGCCGCCCCCGCCCCG) was attached to the 5′ end of the CYA359F primer to improve subsequent denaturant gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) analysis. Using a Mastercycler Pro (Eppendorf AG, Hamburg, Germany), PCR amplifications were performed. Each primer (0.8 μM) was combined with 0.2 mM of each deoxynucleoside triphosphate, 0.25 μg of bovine serum albumin (BSA), 2.5 μL of 10 × PCR buffer (Platinum Taq, Invitrogen Corp., Carlsbad, CA, USA), 0.2 μL DNA polymerase (Platinum Taq, Invitrogen), 3 ng of template DNA, and water to a volume of 25 μL. Thirty-five incubation cycles followed an initial denaturation step (2 min at 94°C), each consisting of 30 s at 94°C, 1 min at 60°C and 1 min at 72°C. Amplified 16S rDNA products (490 bp) were run on a Biorad DCode System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA) using DGGE. Eight-per cent polyacrylamide gels with an internal gradient of 30–65% denaturants (urea and formamide) were poured following the manufacturer’s instructions (Biorad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA). Wells were rinsed with unpolymerised acrylamide before loading. An aliquot of 7 μL of the PCR product was loaded using 7 μL 2 × DGGE loading dye (2 mL DCode dye solution, 7 mL glycerol, and 1 mL dH₂O) in a 1 : 1 ratio. Gels were run at 100V for 14 h, stained for 20–35 min using SYBR Green I (Molecular Probes Inc., Amresco), 10 000 × diluted in 0.5 × Tris-acetate-ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (TAE), and photographed using a digital camera fitted with a SYBR green filter. Bands were picked out of the gel using a pipette tip that was placed in 30 μL of water for 4 h at room temperature. An aliquot of 3 μL of the template DNA from each band was amplified in another PCR reaction (same as above), using the primers CYA359F (without the GC clamp) and CYA781R. Amplified DNA was run on 1% agarose gel and DNA bands were cut out and purified using an UltraClean 15 DNA purification kit (Mo Bio Laboratories Inc., Carlsbad, CA, USA). Purified DNA was sequenced by a DNA big dye terminator (BDT) labelling reaction, followed by capillary separation (Australian Genome Research Facility Ltd, Brisbane, Australia), using both CYA359F (without the GC clamp) and CYA781R primers in separate reactions. Sequences were blasted against the GenBank database and identified as the best matching sequence (>98%). Homology was determined using BLAST 1.8.3-Paracel (14 June 2009) (Altschul et al. 1997). The sequences were deposited in GenBank and assigned accession numbers.

Data analysis
Regression was used to determine the rates of nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat and sediment with the overlying water over time. ANOVA was used to test for differences in N-fixation rates for day v. night and low v. high intertidal zones, with time of the day and position in the intertidal zone being fixed effects in the model. Normality was assessed and confirmed using normality probability plots and D’Agostino Pearson omnibus K2 tests. Analyses were performed using the packages Statistica (Version 8, StatSoft, Tulsa, OK, USA) and Prism, 5.0 (GraphPad, La Jolla, CA, USA). Throughout the results section, data are presented as mean ± standard error.

Results

Nutrient exchange during tidal inundation

During field experiments, concentrations of NO\(_x^-\)-N and NH\(_4^+\) decreased as the tidal cycle progressed (Fig. 2). The decrease in NO\(_x^-\)-N was pronounced, with concentrations almost halved as the tidal cycle progressed, with a rate of \(-1.3 \pm 0.58\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) and a decrease in concentration from 15 \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) at the beginning of the flood tide to \(\sim 7\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) at the end of the ebb tide. The regression for NO\(_x^-\)-N decrease over time was significant (\(R^2 = 0.39\), \(F_{1,10} = 6.27\), \(P = 0.031\)). Concentrations of NH\(_4^+\) also decreased over a tidal cycle, although clearly only during one tidal cycle, when concentrations decreased from 60 \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) at the beginning of the flood to \(\sim 30\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) on the ebb tide, with a rate of \(-6.8\) \(\mu\)g L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\). The concentrations of SRP throughout a tidal cycle were more variable, increasing in some tidal cycles and decreasing in others (Fig. 2). Overall, during our field experiments, the cyanobacterial mat removed nutrients from the floodwater, contrary to our first hypothesis (H1), which predicted that nutrients were released to the floodwater during tidal inundation.

Nutrient exchange in chambers

In the nutrient-chamber experiments, we observed results similar to those of the field experiments. During the experiment, NO\(_x^-\)-N concentrations decreased in the chambers with cyanobacterial mat, whereas NH\(_4^+\) concentrations decreased not only in the chambers with cyanobacterial mat but also in the chambers with sediment only. Concentrations of SRP did not significantly change during our experiments. The removal of NO\(_x^-\)-N and NH\(_4^+\) by the cyanobacterial mat occurred only in light conditions. Sediment without mat removed NH\(_4^+\) during dark conditions (Fig. 3, Table 1). The chamber experiments provided evidence that supports our second hypothesis (H2) that nutrient exchange in cyanobacterial mats is higher in the day than at night.

When comparing desiccated and wet cyanobacterial mats, concentrations of NO\(_x^-\)-N, NH\(_4^+\) and SRP decreased in both treatments as soon as the experiment started (Fig. 4, Table 1). All the regressions for the removal of nutrients over time in this experiment were significant (\(P < 0.01\)) (Table 1). There was no difference between the nutrient exchange of the wet and the desiccated cyanobacterial mats. Thus, regardless of previous desiccation, the cyanobacterial mat removed nutrients from the floodwater during tidal inundation.

In general, nutrient concentrations in the blank samples (containing only filtered seawater) did not change considerably during the course of the experiments. However, in the last experiment (desiccated v. wet, Fig. 4), the NH\(_4^+\) concentration decreased in the control chamber, in addition to declines observed in the chambers with cyanobacterial mat. Furthermore, during the experiments conducted in the light, the initial NO\(_x^-\)-N concentrations in the blank chamber were much lower than those in the chambers with the cyanobacterial mat and sediment only, which suggests a release of NO\(_x^-\)-N to the water column as soon as the cyanobacterial mat and sediment chambers were flooded (Figs 3, 4).

Nitrogen fixation

The mean N fixation rate was \(1.7 \pm 0.26\) nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\) (\(4.9 \pm 0.77\) nmol C\(_2\)H\(_2\) N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)). In comparison, the removal of N from the floodwater was 3.2 nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). Thus, N fixation accounts for 34% of total N incorporation, a result that supports our third hypothesis that N fixation is a significant component of N incorporation into the cyanobacterial mat. N-fixation rates were higher during the day (\(2.7 \pm 0.36\) nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\); \(8.0 \pm 1.1\) nmol C\(_2\) H\(_2\) N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) than at night (\(1.1 \pm 0.34\) nmol N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\); \(3.2 \pm 1.0\) nmol C\(_2\) H\(_2\) N cm\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\)) (\(F_{1,9} = 19.2\), \(P = 0.002\)) (Table 2), a result that rejects our fourth hypothesis (H4). N-fixation rates in the lower intertidal zone were higher than those in the higher intertidal zone (\(F_{1,4} = 11.1\), \(P = 0.03\)), supporting our fifth hypothesis (H5).

Composition of the cyanobacterial mat

Visual observations of mat samples by light microscopy revealed that the majority of the mat structure was composed of

sheaths of filamentous species that no longer contained living cells. The living cells were non-heterocystous forms within the Oscillatoriaceae, including representatives of the genera Oscillatoria and Microcoleus (Table 3). Coccoid cells appeared to be more abundant in the low intertidal-zone samples, whereas filamentous forms were dominant in the high intertidal zone.

The 16s rDNA sequencing returned nine species, four from the low intertidal-zone samples and six from the high intertidal-zone samples (Fig. 5, Table 3). Microcoleus chthonoplastes occurred in both the low and high intertidal-zone samples. In the low intertidal zone, Oscillatoria sp. was also recovered with two unidentified species that showed less than 98% similarity to the closest match in the GenBank database. In the high intertidal-zone samples, the community comprised a range of species from the Oscillatoriaceae, including Plectonema sp., Lyngbya aestuarii, Geitlerniema sp. and Leptolyngbya sp. Overall, we found some evidence of differential composition of the cyanobacterial mat across the intertidal zone, supporting H6.

Discussion
Nutrient exchange during tidal inundation
Contrary to our first hypothesis, during our field experiments cyanobacterial mat removed nutrients, especially N (NO\(_x^-\)-N and NH\(_4^+\)), from the floodwater during tidal inundation. Our field and experimental data showed that even when the cyanobacterial mat was previously desiccated, it removed nutrients when it was flooded. However, some evidence of N release was also found. Initial NO\(_x^-\)-N concentrations in the blank chamber were lower than initial concentrations for the cyanobacterial mat and sediment chambers. As the initial seawater was the same for all the chambers, it appears that the cyanobacterial mat and the sediment released NO\(_x^-\)-N to the water column as soon as they were flooded. This observation suggests that the cyanobacterial mat may release nutrients to the floodwater at the beginning of the flood tide. After being submerged for some time, the cyanobacterial mat becomes completely functional and assimilates nutrients from the floodwater.

In our experiments, NH\(_4^+\) was removed from the floodwater not only in the cyanobacterial mat but also in the sediment without cyanobacterial mat. This result could be explained by chemical adsorption of NH\(_4^+\) to the sediment, or that the sediment without a cyanobacterial mat is covered with thin biofilms, where various microorganisms, including nitrifying bacteria, may occur (Decho 2000). Nitrifying bacteria from intertidal sediments are capable of removing NH\(_4^+\) from the floodwater (Bohlool et al. 1977), which can then be oxidised to NO\(_3^-\). and nitrification are usually tightly coupled (Paerl and Pinckney 1996). The processes responsible for the nutrient removal from the floodwater that we observed could include biological assimilation, nitrification and denitrification. However, in intertidal mudflats, assimilation is much more important than denitrification in incorporating N from the floodwater (Cook et al. 2004). Thus, it is likely that most of the nutrient removal from the floodwater by the cyanobacterial mat is due to biological assimilation. The spatial and temporal variation of each component process involved in the removal and release of N in cyanobacterial mats, although beyond the scope of the present paper, should be explored to fully understand nutrient exchange of cyanobacterial mats during tidal inundation.

Our results differ from results reported for a location close to our sampling site (Dampier Archipelago, 200 km north of the Exmouth Gulf) by Paling and McComb (1994) who found that N was released from the cyanobacterial mat. The difference in the direction of N fluxes from both studies highlights the temporal and spatial variability of nutrient exchange of cyanobacterial mats during tidal inundation. During our field experiments, unusually heavy rain was falling in the area, which strongly modified the environment by causing flooding and increasing the amounts of nutrients in the floodwater. Thus, the results from the present study are likely to represent nutrient exchange of cyanobacterial mats during tropical storms or similar weather events. An increase in N and SRP in the floodwater could have increased the growth of the cyanobacterial mat and, hence, nutrient assimilation (Joye and Paerl 1993). Furthermore, nutrient additions can also alter the function of the cyanobacterial mat from an autotrophic–heterotrophic balance to pure autotrophic, by increasing primary productivity and possibly modifying the benthic community composition (Porubsky et al. 2008).

High N-removal rates from the floodwater occurred mainly under light conditions, a result that confirms our second hypothesis (H2). Removal of nutrients under light conditions is likely to be a result of higher activity and metabolic demands of the mat during the day. Light and dark comparisons may have been confounded by differences in nutrient concentrations of the seawater used for each experiment because of nutrient pulses associated with the approaching cyclone, which may affect nutrient assimilation (Saunders and Kalff 2001). However, similar results of cyanobacterial mat assimilating N (NO\(_3^-\) and NH\(_4^+\)) at greater rates in light than in dark conditions have previously been reported in temperate cyanobacterial mats in Georgia, USA (Porubsky et al. 2008).

Cyanobacterial mat composition
Our visual observations of the mat community showed that the cyanobacterial mat in the Exmouth Gulf is composed mainly of sheaths, probably derived from species from the Oscillatoriales. Sheaths of cyanobacteria generally preserve well compared with other structures (Bartley 1996), which explains their abundance and high contribution to the structure of the mat.

There was a clear difference in the morphology of the living cells from the high and low intertidal samples. Although we found Microcoleus sp. in both the low and high intertidal zones, the low intertidal-zone samples had abundant coccoid cells, whereas the high intertidal-zone samples had abundant filamentous forms. The cyanobacterial 16s rDNA analysis confirmed the identity and presence of M. chthonoplastes. Low intertidal-zone samples also had Oscillatoria spp. Two bands were also observed that did not show high homology with other published cyanobacterial sequences. Our results provided some evidence that differing communities, or at least morphologies, of cyanobacteria are found across the intertidal zone (H6).

The cyanobacteria composition described in the present study is similar to that in the north-western Dampier Archipelago (200 km north), where Microcoleus chthonoplastes and Geitlerniema sp. (previously Phormidium sp.) were also found (Paling et al. 1989). Our study adds to this species list of cyanobacteria in these arid-zone estuaries, with the occurrence of Plectonema sp., Leptolyngbya sp. and Lyngbya aestuarii in the high intertidal-zone samples.

Nitrogen fixation
The mean N fixation was 1.7 ± 0.33 nmol N cm⁻² h⁻¹, accounting for 34% of total N incorporated by the cyanobacterial mat (N fixation plus N removal during tidal inundation). This result confirms that N fixation is an important mechanism for N incorporation by the cyanobacterial mat in this region (H3). It is probable that N fixation is performed by Oscillatoria sp., Plectonema sp., Leptolyngbya sp., Lyngbya aestuarii, Geitlerniema sp. and Microcoleus. However, Leptolyngbya can fix N only if associated with heterotrophic bacteria (Li et al. 2010).

Our results indicated that cyanobacterial mats in Exmouth Gulf are capable of fixing N during the day and at night, with higher rates during the day. Thus, our hypothesis that N-fixation rates were highest at night (H4) was rejected. Diurnal N fixation would suggest the presence of heterocystous cells because of the fact that N fixation is very sensitive to oxygen, which is produced during photosynthesis. However, the species we found in the mat are non-heterocystous forms. Nevertheless, some species of non-heterocystous cyanobacteria have alternative mechanisms that allow them to fix N during both night and day, in both anaerobic and aerobic conditions. Such mechanisms include microanaerobiosis (e.g. Plectonema; Berman-Frank et al. 2003), cellular differentiation (e.g. Trichodesmus; Berman-Frank et al. 2003) or intracellular processes still to be understood (e.g. Lyngbya; Jones 1992), such as inclusion granules (Cyanothece; Reddy et al. 1993). Some species of Plectonema that lack heterocysts have been observed to require light to fix N (Misra and Rakesh 1994). Thus, the occurrence of Plectonema and Lyngbya in the high intertidal zone suggest that these species may be responsible for diurnal N fixation.

As hypothesised (H5), the cyanobacterial mat from the low intertidal zone had higher N-fixation rates than did the cyanobacterial mat at higher intertidal elevations. These results indicated that the biogeochemical function of the cyanobacterial mat varies over the intertidal zone. The difference in N-fixation rates between the low and high intertidal zones could be related to lower salinities and more frequent tidal flushing in the low intertidal zone, which favour N fixation (Paling et al. 1989; Toledo et al. 1995; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). Differences in N fixation between cyanobacterial mats from the low and high intertidal zones might also be a consequence of different cyanobacterial community compositions along the desiccation gradient, as has been observed in a subtropical arid wetland in Baja California Sur, Mexico (Rothrock and Garcia-Pichel 2005) and is suggested in the present study. Variation in N-fixation rates over tidal elevation has also been reported for an intertidal bank in the Wadden Sea (Severin and Stal 2008).

Our results showed that N fixation is temporally and spatially variable and suggested a significant role of N fixation in this ecosystem. The N-fixation rates we measured in our study site (ranging from 1.4 to 8.2 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹, mean 4.9 ± 0.77 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹) were similar to those in cyanobacterial mats in Dampier, Western Australia (0.8–6 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Paling et al. 1989), lower than those found in intertidal mudflats in California, USA (37 nmol C₂H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Joye and Paerl 1994), within the range of those found in the intertidal zone of the lagoon of Aladabra Atoll (0.6–125 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Potts and Whitton 1977) and higher than those measured in mangrove sediments in Zanzibar (0.001 nmol C₂ H₂ cm⁻² h⁻¹; Kyaruzi et al. 2003). Thus, N fixation at our study site could be considerable, especially because of the large areas (>100 km²) occupied by cyanobacterial mats in this region.

The results from the present study have provided insights into the role of cyanobacterial mats in nutrient exchange in coastal arid wetlands during periods of rainfall. The conditions in which we conducted our experiment were very different from conditions that occur most frequently in the region because of the increase in nutrients associated with the rain brought by Cyclone Pancho. The rain and flooding could have strongly modified the nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat. For example, although the N-fixation rates measured were very similar to those measured by Paling et al. (1989), they are likely to be underestimated, as the increased N input resulting from runoff during the tropical cyclone reduces N-fixation rates (Joye and Paerl 1993). Nutrient assimilation during tidal exchange may have also been particularly high during the sampling period because an increase in nutrients enhances assimilation (Joye and Paerl 1993). Thus, the contribution of N fixation to total N incorporation under normal conditions could be higher than the one reported in the present study. Furthermore, the acetylene–ethylene method used to measure N fixation has some limitations, including (1) the relatively long time required to achieve a high, stable ethylene production, (2) the inhibition of acetylene reduction at high acetylene partial pressures and (3) incomplete saturation sites for ethylene production at low partial pressures (Patriquin and Denike 1978). The acetylene–ethylene reduction method can also overestimate N-fixation rates because it measures gross N fixation, without taking into account N loss by other processes such as denitrification (Howarth et al. 1988; Mahaffey et al. 2005). Although we maintained standard conditions between runs (6 h, 25°C), adding confidence to our relative comparisons (low v. high in the intertidal; day v. night), there is potential for error in our comparison of N fixation with N incorporation during tidal inundation. N exchange are highly likely, and further studies will be necessary to characterise the ecosystem contribution of nutrient exchange of the cyanobacterial mat in the Exmouth Gulf.

In conclusion, the results from the present study show that during periods of rainfall, the cyanobacterial mat in this subtropical and arid coastal wetland incorporates N through N fixation and through removal of dissolved nutrients from the floodwater during tidal inundation. The biogeochemical function of the cyanobacterial mat varies spatially and temporally. Spatially, the cyanobacterial mat has higher N-fixation rates in the low than in the high intertidal zone; temporally, it removes more nutrients from the floodwater and fixes more N in the day than at night. The cyanobacterial mat removes nutrients from the tidal water as soon as it is flooded, regardless of previous desiccation. The composition of the cyanobacterial mat in Giralia Bay is characterised by non-heterocystous forms within the Oscillatoriaceae, including representatives of the genera Oscillatoria and Microcoleus, whereas composition of the mat varies with elevation; more species are likely to occur in the high intertidal zone.

As predicted by McKinnon and Ayukai (1996), the vast cyanobacterial mats in Exmouth Gulf are likely to contribute to nutrient exchange, especially N fluxes, between the intertidal and subtidal ecosystems. The active nutrient exchange and high abundance of cyanobacterial mats in the region are likely to result in a significant contribution to N dynamics at an ecosystem scale, although this remains to be investigated. The exchange between cyanobacterial mats and the coastal ocean could be especially important in arid oligotrophic regions, such as the one in the present study, where cyanobacterial mats could have significant effects on coastal primary and secondary production.

Epilithic nitrogen fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi, Africa Abstract—Rates of epilithic N₂ fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi, determined by in situ incubations and the acetylene reduction method, declined with depth, were highly correlated to light intensity and heterocyst biovolume, and are among the highest observed values for freshwater or marine systems. Daytime N₂ fixation rates were similar between sites at similar depths, except at sediment and nutrient impacted sites, where rates were lower and more variable. Daytime N₂ fixation rates were measurable in all transparent chambers and were negligible in opaque chambers, which indicates that phototrophic diazotrophs (organisms capable of utilizing atmospheric nitrogen) were responsible for all daytime N₂ fixation. Nocturnal N₂ fixation was ~60% of daytime fixation. A model that integrated N₂ fixation over depth and time predicted that epilithic N₂ fixation may contribute up to 35% of N inputs to the epilimnion of Lake Malawi. Lake Malawi is a large (28,000 km²), deep (>700 m) oligotrophic African rift valley lake located between latitudes 9°5'S and 14°5'S. Although only 30% of the shoreline is composed of rocky substrata, approximately one half of Lake Malawi’s 500–1,000+ species of fish reside in the rocky littoral areas (Reinthal 1990; Ribbink et al. 1983), making it a critical habitat for fish biodiversity. The vast majority of these fish are herbivorous, and both ecological studies (Reinthal 1990) and stable isotope studies (Bootsma et al. 1996) indicate that epilithic periphyton is the most important component of their diets. Photosynthetic rates by the epilithic periphyton of Lake Malawi reach maximum values near 1g C m⁻² d⁻¹, which are similar to those that occur on coral reefs (Bootsma 1993). However, rates of nutrient uptake for these algal communities are unknown. The dominance of heterocystous cyanoprokaryotes within the epilithic periphyton community, and recent evidence that ambient total nitrogen concentrations are among the lowest for freshwater or marine systems (~7 μM; Guildford & Hecky 2000), suggest that the process of nitrogen fixation could play an important role in supplying “new” nitrogen to the epilithic periphyton community and epilimnion of Lake Malawi. The purpose of this study was, first, to determine the spatial dynamics of epilithic N₂ fixation in the rocky littoral zones of Lake Malawi and to estimate its contribution to the N requirements of the epilithic periphyton community. Such information is necessary for a more complete understanding of the factors that control periphyton productivity, which in turn maintains the dense and diverse littoral fish community of Lake Malawi. Second, this study examines the relationships between epilithic N₂ fixation, heterocyst biovolume, light intensity, and chlorophyll concentration, in an attempt to identify the controlling factors and variability in epilithic N₂ fixation rates. Third, this study gives preliminary estimates for the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation in the whole lake nitrogen budget of Lake Malawi and compares rates in Lake Malawi with freshwater and marine habitats over a wide range of latitudes. Sites—To accomplish the study objectives, five rocky littoral zone sites were selected in the central and southern portions of Lake Malawi. All experiments were conducted during the dry windy seasons (May–October) of 1997 and 1998. During 1997, two sites were used for study (Maleri South and Maleri North). Because of the presence of crocodiles at these sites during 1998, these sites were abandoned, and experiments were conducted at three new sites (Likoma Island [LI]-Makalawe, LI-Membe, and Thumbi West) during 1998. A more detailed description of the physical habitat at these sites was presented in Higgins (1999) and Ribbink et al. (1983). On average, each site/depth was sampled 2–3 times monthly, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and LI-Membe, which were opportunistically sampled over a 2-d period during May 1998. Acetylene reduction assays—Epilithic nitrogen fixation was estimated by modification of the acetylene reduction technique (Stewart et al. 1967) to allow for sampling epilithic periphyton communities, in situ, over a depth gradient (2–16 m) by use of SCUBA diving. The modifications are described in detail in Higgins (1999) and include the use of 800-ml, opaque, and ultraviolet-transparent plexiglass chambers fitted with a neoprene seal and skirt and weighted with a lead sock to isolate chamber water from surrounding ambient water. Chambers were placed on rocky surfaces, injected with 100 ml (at surface temperature and pressure) of welder’s-grade acetylene, stirred vigorously by use of a built-in stirring device, and incubated for 0.5–2.5 h. After the incubation time, the chamber was stirred vigorously, and a 40-ml aqueous sample was taken by use of a glass 50-ml syringe fitted with a three-way valve. After 10 ml of surface air was drawn in, the syringe was shaken vigorously for 2 min and placed in a water bath (at lake temperature) for ~1 min before the headspace was drawn into a 7-ml vacutainer, which was later analyzed on a Shimadzu GC-8A chromatograph fitted with a 3.05 m × 6.35 mm × 5.34 mm Altech porasil C/phenyl isocyanate mesh 80/100 column. Calibration with ethylene standards was conducted both prior to and after sample analysis each day, and an interlab calibration with known ethylene concentrations and 25 random samples (Freshwater Institute, Winnipeg, Canada). A time-series experiment was conducted, and rates of ethylene production were found to be linear between 0.5 and 2.5 h. Rates of N₂ fixation were calculated by use of a theoretical 4 : 1 (C₂H₂ : N₂) conversion ratio, which is of similar magnitude to experimentally determined conversion ratios for epilithic algal communities (Reuter et al. 1986; Larkum et al. 1988). In several acetylene reduction assays, screens of different mesh sizes were placed over the chambers, to reduce the amount of solar radiation received by the periphyton com- Table 1. The amount of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) received by the algal communities within each chamber was calculated from in situ light readings, combined with the percentage of transmission through each screen, calculated by use of a LICOR LI-1800 Spectroradiometer within a tub of lake water under low wave conditions. The in situ light readings were taken concurrent to, and directly beside, the acetylene reduction assays by use of a LICOR LI-1000 Data Logger and Quantum Sensor with a flat plate collector. Algal collection, heterocyst enumeration, and chlorophyll—After most experiments, duplicate or triplicate algal samples were taken from the rock surface within each chamber by use of a periphyton-scraping device, as described by Loeb (1981). The periphyton samples were stored in the dark and returned to the laboratory, where subsamples were taken for chlorophyll a analysis and heterocyst enumeration. Chl a was extracted from filtered subsamples at −5°C for ~14 h by use of an alkaline acetone solution, according to the methods of Stainton et al. (1977), and analyzed fluorometrically. For each site and depth combination, five algal samples were randomly chosen for heterocyst enumeration. A 2-ml subsample was placed in a Utermöhl chamber, and at least 50 fields (or 100 heterocysts) were counted by use of a Zeiss Axioinvert 35 inverted phase microscope with 400× magnification. Each sample to be counted was selected randomly, such that the person counting did not know the site or depth from which it originated. Daytime N₂ fixation—During daylight hours, rates of nitrogen fixation were easily detectable in all transparent chambers (Table 1), whereas rates in opaque chambers were typically 4%–7% of rates in transparent chambers, which indicates that photosynthetic cyanoprokaryotes were responsible for the majority N₂ fixation rates noted. The dominance of heterocystous forms of Calothrix at virtually all sites and depths studied (Higgins 1999) make it highly probable that they were responsible for the majority of daytime N₂ fixation by the periphyton community. Cyanoprokaryotic endosymbionts capable of N₂ fixation were found in several species of the diatom Rhopalodia; however, their total biovolume was generally an order of magnitude less than Calothrix heterocyst biovolume (Higgins 1999); therefore, they likely do not contribute largely to the overall fixation rates noted. The range of daytime N₂ fixation rates was 1–2,920 \( \mu \)g N m⁻² h⁻¹, with variability generally <30% of the mean value for each site/depth (Table 1). The Maleri Island sites, which are known to be impacted annually by a plume of sediment- and nutrient-rich water extending from the nearby Linthipe River (Bootsma and Hecky 1999), are an exception and have much higher variability, especially at 10 m depth. At the Maleri South site, a 1–2 cm layer of silt covering rocky surfaces was noted below 7 m depth, and rocky surfaces had a relatively low total standing crop of periphyton and biovolume of heterocysts (Higgins 1999). Nitrogen fixation, Chl a, and heterocyst biovolume—Of the parameters known to influence N₂ fixation, the strongest correlation was found with heterocyst biovolume (\( R = 0.71, P < 0.005 \); Fig. 1) and solar insolation (discussed below). Both N₂ fixation rates and heterocyst biovolume showed generally decreasing values with increasing depth at all sites sampled (Fig. 2a–e, Table 1). In contrast to studies on the epilithic periphyton of five northern temperate lakes by Loeb and Reuter (1981), chlorophyll and N₂ fixation were not highly correlated in the epilithic periphyton of Lake Malawi (\( R = 0.04, P = 0.70 \)). Studies on coral reefs have shown an inverse relationship between N₂ fixation and chlorophyll, which was attributed to the grazing activity of fish keeping the periphyton community in an early succesional stage, decreasing chlorophyll concentrations while increasing rates of primary production and nitrogen fixation (Wilkinson and Sammarco 1983; Larkum 1988). This may also be the case in Lake Malawi, where densities of grazing fish can exceed 10 individuals m⁻² area (Ribbink et al. 1983). Nitrogen fixation versus light model—The results of the screen experiments indicated that rates of nitrogen fixation per heterocyst were strongly dependent on the amount of PAR reaching the periphyton community (\( R^2 = 0.75, P < 0.001 \); Fig. 3). Nonlinear regression was used to fit these data to the relationship modified from Platt et al. (1980) by Lewis and Levine (1984), \[ N = N_s (1 - e^{-(\alpha I / N_s)}) e^{-(\beta I / N_s)} + D, \] where \( N \) is the amount of nitrogen fixed per heterocyst biovolume per unit time, \( N_s \) is the parameter representing maximum nitrogen fixation per heterocyst biovolume in the absence of light inhibition, \( I \) is the light intensity (PAR), \( \alpha \) is the slope of the light-limited and linear part of the N-fixation versus PAR curve, \( \beta \) is the parameter for light inhibition, and \( D \) is the fixation rate for heterocysts in the dark (Levine and Lewis 1987). Because light inhibition of nitrogen fixation under high light intensities was not evident during any of the experiments and fixation rates in the dark (during daylight hours) were negligible, the parameters \( \beta \) and \( D \) were set to zero. The N_2 fixation model, which integrates the relationships between N_2 fixation per heterocyst versus light, solar irradiance, light extinction, and heterocyst biovolume can be used in simulations to calculate N_2 fixation over a wide variety of spatial and temporal ranges. The \( R^2 \) value refers to the relationship between in situ screen measurements (dots) and the N-fixation equation (line) modified from Platt et al. (1980). solar insolation), and 1 January 1997 (rainy season, highest solar insolation), were calculated by use of a mean light extinction coefficient of 0.2 (\( n = 18 \), range 0.16–0.25), cloudless solar data generated by Fee’s (1990) model (14°S latitude), and the relationship between heterocyst biovolume and depth (Higgins 1999). This simulation predicts that the maximum difference in nitrogen fixation rates due to seasonal differences in solar radiation is ~15% of the annual mean value. The 1 June 1997 simulation was also used to compare model estimates with in situ estimates of hourly N_2 fixation at midday for 2, 5, and 10 m depths (Table 1, Fig. 2f). The 1 June 1997 simulation for 2 m depth predicted a N_2 fixation rate of 1,490 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, which fell within the range of N_2 fixation rates for each site, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and Thumbi West (Table 1, Fig. 2f) and agreed with the site-averaged in situ N_2 fixation rate of 1,500 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. The model predicted values of 910 and 370 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1} for 5 and 10 m depths, which agreed closely with the site-averaged in situ estimates of 950 and 410 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. Patch-specific and nocturnal rates of nitrogen fixation— Above 1 m depth at all sites, and from 0–5 m depth at Maleri South, visually distinct patches of epilithic periphyton dominated by Calothrix or Cladophora were observed throughout the sampling season (May–October). At other sites and depths, the epilithic periphyton community was more homogenous and was dominated by heterocystous Calothrix spp (Higgins 1999; Higgins unpubl. data). The biomass of Calothrix patches were dominated by heterocystous Calothrix species, whereas the biomass of Cladophora patches were codominated by Cladophora, Calothrix, and a variety of epiphytic diatoms (Higgins 1999). Calothrix patches at 2 m depth had significantly higher rates of nitrogen fixation (1,450 ± 540 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}; \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) than Cladophora patches (720 ± 90 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) during daylight hours (\( t \)-test, \( P = 0.03 \)). The relative patchiness in the epilithic periphyton community structure at shallow depths of the Maleri Island sites is likely responsible for the higher variability in N_2 fixation rates noted (Table 1), whereas the impacts of sediment accumulation account for the high variability at deeper depths. The mean rate of nocturnal nitrogen fixation in Calothrix patches, from 1–2 m depth, was double that for Cladophora patches, was ~60% of the daytime averages for nitrogen fixation (Tables 1, 2), and was an order of magnitude larger than rates measured in opaque chambers during the day. Although the difference in N_2 fixation rates between daytime dark box and nocturnal dark box experiments was unexpected, there are a number of plausible explanations. First, nocturnal N_2 fixation by nonheterocystous diazotrophs might occur primarily at night, when O_2 inhibition is reduced (i.e., the temporal separation of N_2 fixation and O_2 evolution processes). Second, the length of incubation during daytime dark box experiments may have been insufficient to allow a shift in adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and reductant pathways, which differ between day and night within heterocystous diazotrophs (Stewart 1973). The agreement between model estimates and in situ estimates for N₂ fixation allowed us to estimate daytime N₂ fixation throughout the littoral zone. From a maximal carbon fixation rate of 1 g m⁻² d⁻¹ (Bootsma 1993) and a “Redfield” C : N ratio of 5.68 (molar), the calculated 24-h N demand of periphyton would be 170 mg N m⁻² d⁻¹. From model estimates of daily N₂ fixation at shallow depths (1–2 m), N₂ fixation would contribute between 8% and 12% of the total 24-hr N demand of epilithic periphyton and between 13% and 18% if nocturnal N₂ fixation were included. To estimate the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation to the N budget of Lake Malawi, we employed our model to spatially and temporally integrate N₂ fixation rates over a depth gradient (under the assumption of a 45° slope) for a single year. Within the model, we multiplied area estimates over a range of factors (2–5.7), to adjust for roughness of the substrata (Higgins 1999), then extrapolated the results over the entire rocky littoral zone area in Lake Malawi, as determined from literature sources (Ribbink et al. 1983) and aerial surveys (Cooley unpubl. data). Although our model uses estimated daily PAR under 100% cloudless conditions from Fee’s (1990) model, we calculated depth-integrated rates under 70% cloudless conditions and found only a 10% difference in model output (due to light saturation at shallow depths). On the basis of these assumptions, the N₂ fixation model estimates that 4–20 × 10⁴ kg N lake⁻¹ yr⁻¹, or 40–120 mmol N m⁻² yr⁻¹, is biologically fixed by epilithic diazotrophs. This estimate for epilithic N₂ fixation is similar in magnitude to those for precipitation and riverine inputs to Lake Malawi and suggests that epilithic N₂ fixation may be a significant source of N to the epilimnion (Table 3). Furthermore, because epilithic N₂ fixation rates do not vary substantially between seasons, the relative importance of epilithic N₂ fixation increases during the dry-windy season, when riverine and atmospheric inputs of N and pelagic N₂ fixation are much reduced. Interlake comparisons—Because this study represents the first epilithic N₂ fixation estimates from a tropical lake, epilithic N₂ fixation rates from Lake Malawi are presented along with benthic N₂ fixation rates from both marine and freshwater ecosystems that encompass a wide latitudinal range (Table 4). Summertime hourly N₂ fixation rates do not appear to follow a strong latitudinal gradient for freshwater systems. During the summer insolation period, somewhat lower hour- ly rates in temperate regions are made up for by longer day lengths. As a result, daily rates in arctic regions (during summer months) may be similar to those in more temperate or tropical regions. Because of seasonal differences in solar irradiance patterns and water temperature, however, annual N\(_2\) fixation rates in tropical regions are often an order of magnitude higher than those in temperate regions. Nonetheless, the importance of benthic N\(_2\) fixation to the nitrogen budget in these systems is related to seasonal trends in primary production and N demand and therefore does not necessarily vary over latitudes. For example, Bergmann and Welch (1990) estimated that N\(_2\) fixation accounted for up to 28% of the N budget in some arctic lakes, similar to our estimates for the epilithon of Lake Malawi (Table 3). Epilithic N\(_2\) fixation rates do not show any strong differences between freshwater and marine habitats. Hourly, daily, and annual N\(_2\) fixation rates in the rocky littoral areas of Lake Malawi are similar to those in coral reef habitats. This similarity in N\(_2\) fixation can be at least partially attributed to similarities in primary productivity (Bootsma 1993), grazing rates (Wilkinson and Sammarco 1983; Larkum et al. 1988; Andre 1999), and nutrient availability (Howarth et al. 1988; Bootsma and Hecky 1999). We conclude that benthic nitrogen fixation is a quantitatively significant contribution to the nitrogen requirement of the epilithic periphyton and to dependant herbivores, as well as to the whole-lake nitrogen budget. The predictive model of N\(_2\) fixation should be tested through further studies on Lake Malawi and other tropical lakes. Scott N. Higgins,1 Robert E. Hecky, and William D. Received: 1 March 2000 Accepted: 5 March 2001 Amended: 12 March 2001 High-resolution metal gradients measured by in situ DGT/DET deployment in Black Sea sediments using an autonomous benthic lander Abstract—DET (Diffusive equilibration in thin films) and DGT (diffusive gradients in thin films) have been deployed in situ using an autonomous benthic lander to measure concentrations and induced fluxes of Fe and Mn (DET/DGT) and trace metals (DGT) in pore waters at millimeter spatial resolutions. The newly developed deployment system is described, and based on these first results, its strengths and weaknesses are discussed. Deployments were made in the Western Black Sea in shelf sediments overlain by well-oxygenated water at a water depth of 77 m. Maxima of the redox-sensitive metals at 4 and 8 cm deep within the sediment indicated that two zones of reduction dominated the geochemistry. Sharp, but systematic, features were superimposed on this general picture and were well replicated in the profiles of Mn, Co, and Cd, but the sharp features in the Fe profile were offset from those of the others elements by several millimeters. Detection of this functional discrimination between Fe and Mn as regulators of trace metals would not have been possible using more conventional sampling procedures. The sediment–water interface is chemically and microbiologically the most active site in natural waters, with steep gradients in physical, chemical, and biological properties (Santschi et al. 1990). Over the last 20 yr, the spatial resolution of measurements of solute concentrations in pore waters has been improved to a submillimeter scale for a limited range of determinands (e.g. O_2, NO_3^−, pH, pCO_2) through the development of microelectrodes and optrodes (Larsen et al. 1997; Glud et al. 1999). These techniques have demonstrated the existence of concentration gradients across the sediment–water interface over millimeter and submillimeter depth scales (Cai and Reimers 1993). Although the resolution of conventional (Carrignan et al. 1985) slicing/squeezing and dialysis procedures has been improved (Shaw et al. 1990; Aller et al. 1998) and voltametric electrodes have been used for Mn and Fe and other solutes (e.g., I^− and S(−II)) (Bren- del and Luther 1995; Luther et al. 1998), only the emerging techniques of DET (diffusive equilibration in thin films) and DGT (diffusive gradients in thin films) have provided high-resolution data for a wide range of components that include trace metals other than Fe and Mn (Davison et al. 2000). DET is directly comparable to more traditional “peeper” systems, except that diffusive equilibrium is attained between solutes in the pore waters and in a thin film of gel. The thinness (<1 mm) of the film results in much faster diffusive equilibration than with traditional peepers. DET has been used to measure Ca^{2+}, Mg^{2+}, Na^{+}, K^{+}, Fe^{2/3+}, Mn^{2+}, Cl^−, SO_4^{2−}, NO_3^−, alkalinity, and ΣCO_2 in pore waters at a resolution of 1–2 mm (Davison et al. 1994; Brunnegard 1997; Mortimer et al. 1998; Zhang et al. 1999) and Fe at a resolution of 400 μm (Fones et al. 1998) and in two dimensions (Shuttleworth et al. 1999). DGT (Davison et al. 2000) uses an extra backing layer of gel impregnated with chelating resin. Metal continuously diffuses across the outer layer of gel (95% water) and accumulates on the chelating resin. After deployment, the resin gel layer is sliced and eluted with acid, and metals are determined by atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Deployment for a given time at a known temperature allows calculation of the mean flux to the resin gel during deployment. If pore waters are effectively buffered by rapid resupply from a local source, such as a desorbing solid phase, the measured flux can be quantitatively interpreted as a concentration (Zhang et al. 1995; Harper et al. 1998). DET/DGT assemblies were initially deployed in situ in shallow waters by SCUBA divers (Davison et al. 1994; Zhang et al. 1995; Brunnegard 1997) or placed by hand (Davison et al. 1997). The 1 June 1997 simulation for 2 m depth predicted a N_2 fixation rate of 1,490 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, which fell within the range of N_2 fixation rates for each site, with the exception of LI-Makalawe and Thumbi West (Table 1, Fig. 2f) and agreed with the site-averaged in situ N_2 fixation rate of 1,500 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}. Patch-specific and nocturnal rates of nitrogen fixation— Above 1 m depth at all sites, and from 0–5 m depth at Maleri South, visually distinct patches of epilithic periphyton dominated by Calothrix or Cladophora were observed throughout the sampling season (May–October). At other sites and depths, the epilithic periphyton community was more homogenous and was dominated by heterocystous Calothrix spp (Higgins 1999; Higgins unpubl. data). The biomass of Calothrix patches were dominated by heterocystous Calothrix species, whereas the biomass of Cladophora patches were codominated by Cladophora, Calothrix, and a variety of epiphytic diatoms (Higgins 1999). Calothrix patches at 2 m depth had significantly higher rates of nitrogen fixation (1,450 ± 540 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}; \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) than Cladophora patches (720 ± 90 \( \mu \)g N m^{-2} h^{-1}, \( X \pm SD; n = 6 \)) during daylight hours (\( t \)-test, \( P = 0.03 \)). The relative patchiness in the epilithic periphyton community structure at shallow depths of the Maleri Island sites is likely responsible for the higher variability in N_2 fixation rates noted (Table 1), whereas the impacts of sediment accumulation account for the high variability at deeper depths. The mean rate of nocturnal nitrogen fixation in Calothrix patches, from 1–2 m depth, was double that for Cladophora patches, was ~60% of the daytime averages for nitrogen fixation (Tables 1, 2), and was an order of magnitude larger than rates measured in opaque chambers during the day. Although the difference in N_2 fixation rates between daytime dark box and nocturnal dark box experiments was unexpected, there are a number of plausible explanations. First, nocturnal N_2 fixation by nonheterocystous diazotrophs might occur primarily at night, when O_2 inhibition is reduced (i.e., the temporal separation of N_2 fixation and O_2 evolution processes). Second, the length of incubation during daytime dark box experiments may have been insufficient to allow a shift in adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and reductant pathways, which differ between day and night within heterocystous diazotrophs (Stewart 1973). To estimate the importance of epilithic N₂ fixation to the N budget of Lake Malawi, we employed our model to spatially and temporally integrate N₂ fixation rates over a depth gradient (under the assumption of a 45° slope) for a single year. Within the model, we multiplied area estimates over a range of factors (2–5.7), to adjust for roughness of the substrata (Higgins 1999), then extrapolated the results over the entire rocky littoral zone area in Lake Malawi, as determined from literature sources (Ribbink et al. 1983) and aerial surveys (Cooley unpubl. data). Although our model uses estimated daily PAR under 100% cloudless conditions from Fee’s (1990) model, we calculated depth-integrated rates under 70% cloudless conditions and found only a 10% difference in model output (due to light saturation at shallow depths). On the basis of these assumptions, the N₂ fixation model estimates that 4–20 × 10⁴ kg N lake⁻¹ yr⁻¹, or 40–120 mmol N m⁻² yr⁻¹, is biologically fixed by epilithic diazotrophs. This estimate for epilithic N₂ fixation is similar in magnitude to those for precipitation and riverine inputs to Lake Malawi and suggests that epilithic N₂ fixation may be a significant source of N to the epilimnion (Table 3). Furthermore, because epilithic N₂ fixation rates do not vary substantially between seasons, the relative importance of epilithic N₂ fixation increases during the dry-windy season, when riverine and atmospheric inputs of N and pelagic N₂ fixation are much reduced.
