Nitrogen-Fixation Activity and the Abundance and Taxonomy of nifH Genes in Agricultural, Pristine, and Urban Prairie Stream Sediments Chronically Exposed to Different Levels of Nitrogen Loading

I. R. Caton‡, T. M. Caton, and M. A. Schneegurt
Department of Biological Sciences, Wichita State University, Wichita, KS 67260

Abstract
Small streams exert great influences on the retention and attenuation of nitrogen (N) within stream networks. Human land use can lead to increased transport of dissolved inorganic N compounds and downstream eutrophication. Microbial activity in streams is important for maintaining an actively functioning N cycle. Chronically high N loading in streams affects the rates of the central processes of the N cycle by increasing rates of nitrification and denitrification, with biota exhibiting decreased efficiency of N use. The LINXII project measured N-cycle parameters in small streams using \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) tracer release experiments. We concurrently measured N\(_2\) fixation rates in six streams of three types (agricultural, pristine, and urban prairie streams) as part of this broader study of major N cycle processes. Nitrogen fixation in streams was significantly negatively correlated with nitrate levels, dissolved inorganic N levels, and denitrification rates. Algal mat and leaf litter samples generally exhibited the highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation. The abundance of nifH genes, as measured by real-time PCR, was marginally correlated with N\(_2\)-fixation rates, but not to other N cycle processes or stream characteristics. The nifH sequences observed were assigned to cyanobacteria, Deltaproteobacteria, Methylococcus, and Rhizobia. Seasonal changes, disturbances, and varying inputs may encourage a diverse, flexible, stable N\(_2\)-fixing guild. Patchiness in the streams should be considered when assessing the overall impact of N\(_2\) fixation, since algal biomass exhibited high rates of N\(_2\) fixation.

Keywords
Nitrogen fixation; streams; multirate; real-time PCR; nifH

Introduction
Small headwater streams have great influence on the transport of available N downstream, ultimately contributing to the eutrophication of receiving bodies of water (Dodds and Smith 2016). Spiraling theory suggests that control of N transport and cycling downstream are predominantly in-stream biotic uptake and assimilation, including mineralization,

</page>

<page number="1">

nitrification, and denitrification (Dodds et al. 2002; Webster et al. 2003; Mulholland 2004). Urbanization, cropland fertilization, and high-density livestock operations, among other land uses, can lead to increases over pristine streams in chronic levels of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) compounds. Nitrification and denitrification rates increase with increases in chronic NO\(_3^-\) levels in streams, essentially increasing N removal, while keeping transport constant (Kemp and Dodds 2002a).

The current report is part of the nationwide Lotic Inter-site Nitrogen eXperiment II (LINX II) field study at the Konza Prairie Biological Station, an LTER in Kansas, that used whole-stream \(^{15}\)NO\(_3^-\) isotope tracer release techniques to measure N cycle processes in nine small streams with varying levels of chronic N loading (O’Brien et al. 2007; Mulholland et al. 2008, 2009; Hall et al. 2009; Knapp et al. 2009; Bernot et al. 2010; Graham et al. 2010; O’Brien and Dodds 2010). The rates of uptake, nitrification, and denitrification were increased 10\(^{-}\) to 100-fold in response to chronically high N loading. Denitrification represented only a small portion of the total uptake of NO\(_3^-\), but was important in the loss of N. A key finding was that the efficiency of NO\(_3^-\) use by biota decreased with increasing N loading. These findings support the Efficiency Loss model of nutrient dynamics and do not fit a 1st-order linear model where N cycling is tied to DIN, but retention efficiency remains constant across streams despite increasing chronic N loading. While saturation was not observed, even in highly loaded streams, acute additions of high levels of NO\(_3^-\) to stream samples demonstrated that uptake can be saturated by short-term loading (Kemp and Dodds 2002b; O’Brien and Dodds 2010). Ambient levels of DIN in streams were low relative to the saturation levels measured by acute NO\(_3^-\) additions. It was suggested that N limitation is severe and likely limits the growth of microbiota (Kemp and Dodds 2002b; Tank and Dodds 2003; Bernot and Dodds 2005; O’Brien and Dodds 2010).

The role of N\(_2\) fixation in the N budgets of small streams seems to vary. Some studies have shown substantial contributions of N\(_2\) fixation to total N input (Grimm 1987; Howarth et al. 1988a, b; Grimm and Petrone 1997; Arango et al. 2009; Kunza and Hall 2014), while others report little impact of N\(_2\) fixation on stream N budgets (Meyer et al. 1981; Triska et al. 1984; Naiman and Melillo 1984; Francis et al. 1985; Marcarelli et al. 2008). Temperature and light conditions are primary controllers of N fixation (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Grimm and Petrone 1997). In oligotrophic streams with low DIN, N\(_2\) fixation ascends in importance (Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2007; Scott et al. 2009; Lang et al. 2012; Kunza and Hall 2013, 2014). There appears to be interplay between P availability and N\(_2\) fixation in streams, with low P levels limiting N\(_2\) fixation (Schindler et al. 2008; Scott et al. 2009; Kunza and Hall 2013).

We measured N\(_2\)-fixation rates by acetylene reduction and performed molecular analyses of diazotrophic microbial community structure in the sediments of six prairie streams from the LINXII effort at Konza Prairie. Several N cycle processes also were measured contemporaneously by collaborators in streams with a range of chronic N loads. The abundance and identity of diazotrophs in stream sediments were determined using the *nifH* gene, which codes for dinitrogenase reductase, a subunit of the nitrogenase complex (Ueda et al. 1995, Zehr et al. 2003).

Materials and Methods

Site Description and Sample Collection

The Flint Hills region of the Great Plains in Northeast Kansas is a tallgrass prairie used primarily for cattle grazing and agriculture (O’Brien et al. 2007). Two streams were selected from each of three main land-use categories, agricultural, pristine, and urban, and their characteristics are given in Table 1. Kings Creek N4D, North Creek, and Campus Creek were sampled in 2003, with the others sampled in 2004. All analyses were performed near the time of sampling.

Sediment samples were collected cleanly at the start, midpoint, and end of each reach (125 to 300 m; O’Brien et al. 2007). Table 2 provides parameters related to stream N-cycle processes that were measured in conjunction with our study. Sediment samples were collected to a depth of 3-5 cm in ~250-ml Mason jars. Leaf litter and algal mat grab samples were collected haphazardly when observed along a reach. Algal mat samples were collected in 10-ml Vacutainer tubes. Samples for N_2-fixation assays were transported at ambient temperature and assays were begun in the laboratory within a few hours. Subsamples held for molecular analyses were placed in sterile containers, frozen immediately in the field, transported on dry ice, and stored at –80 °C prior to analysis.

Acetylene Reduction Assays of Nitrogen Fixation

The metal lids of the 250-ml jars used for sampling were fitted with rubber septa and sealed with silicone vacuum grease creating gas-tight vessels, the headspace of which were accessed by syringe. Jars were filled to approximately two-thirds with sediments that was covered in a layer (~1 cm) of stream water. Since nitrogenase is sensitive to oxygen, the jars were not left open to the air after collection and the small amount headspace oxygen was rapidly exhausted by microbes in the samples. Upon return to the laboratory, acetylene gas was injected into the headspace of the jars (to ~10% v/v). Algal samples were assayed in Vacutainer tubes. Samples with 2 to 6 replicates were incubated at room temperature in natural light and measurements were taken 1, 3, 7, and 14 d after collection. The weights of the sediment samples (~200 g) were recorded to express N_2 fixation per g sediment. The planar surface of the sediment sample in the Mason jar was similar to the area from which the sample was collected (diameter = 6 cm) and this was used to estimate N_2-fixation rates on an areal basis. Similar estimates were made for algal grab samples.

The conversion of acetylene to ethylene by nitrogenase is used as a surrogate for N_2 fixation (Jensen and Cox 1983). The ethylene content of aliquots (0.2 ml) of the headspace gas from the N_2-fixation assays were determined using the method of Reddy et al. (1993) by gas chromatography (Hewlett Packard 6890) with hydrogen flame ionization detection and a microbore DB5 column. Adjustments were made for the trace amount of ethylene found in the acetylene gas and a standard curve was generated by diluting commercial ethylene gas. We use a conversion factor of 3.8 acetylene molecules reduced per one dinitrogen molecule reduced (Jensen and Cox 1983). Theoretical ratios of 3:1 are often applied to N_2-fixation assays (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Grimm and Petrone 1997; Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh

</page>

<page number="3">

2006), but a 4:1 conversion ratio also has been used (Zehr and Montoya 2007; Kunza and Hall 2014).

Bivariate correlation analyses were performed in SPSS Statistics v23 (IBM) to derive Pearson coefficients through pairwise comparisons of measured processes, environmental conditions, stream parameters, and gene abundances. Numerical data were log-transformed for analysis, unless otherwise stated. Pearson correlations of \( p \leq 0.05 \) were considered to be statistically significant in the 2-tailed analyses routinely performed.

Direct Metagenomic DNA Extraction

DNA was directly extracted from sediment, leaf litter, and algal mat samples using the protocol of Bürgmann et al. (2001) with modifications as followed by Kilmer et al. (2014). Environmental samples (~0.5 g) were processed with a bead-beater and extracted with CTAB buffer, followed by phenol extraction and precipitation with polyethylene glycol before collection by centrifugation, washing, and resuspension in buffer. Purity was assessed spectrophotometrically (Genesys 5) by measuring \( A_{260}/A_{280} \) (DNA to protein) and \( A_{260}/A_{230} \) (DNA to humic acids) ratios.

Gene Counting by Real-time PCR

Real-time PCR was performed (Smart Cycler II; Cepheid Technology) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The reaction mixture contained (per 25 µL-reaction): SYBR Premix EX Taq (2x, TaKara), 12.5 µL; PCR forward and reverse primer (10 µM), 0.5 µL each; template DNA extract (≤400 ng), 2 µL; dH2O, 9.5 µL. The nifH gene primers were UNIFF19F (5′–GCIWTYTYAYGGIAARGGIGG–3′) and NifDN (3′–ADNGCCATCATYTCNCC–5′) generating a 464-bp amplicon (Zehr and McReynolds 1989; Ueda et al. 1995; Zehr et al. 1995). Real-time PCR amplification began with 60 s at 95 °C, followed by 45 cycles of 5 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 50 °C, and 15 s at 72 °C, and finally a hold at 72 °C for 60 s. Samples were assayed three to six times to determine typical deviations between different extracts of the same sample and from different amplifications of a single extract. A universal bacterial 16S rRNA gene primer set, EUB338 (5′–ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG–3′) and EUB518 (5′–ATTACCGCGGCTGG–3′), generated a ~200-bp amplicon with PCR as above with 40 s annealing at 53 °C (Fierer et al. 2005). Negative controls were sterile dH2O and a positive control, Cyanothecae sp. str. ATCC 51142 genomic DNA, was used to construct standard curves of gene copy number. The threshold value was 30 fluorescence units and C_t was calculated by the instrument. PCR products were confirmed using 2% agarose gel electrophoresis. Melting curves demonstrated high quality real-time PCR products.

Potential inhibition PCR by contaminants in DNA extracts was assessed using an exogenously added kanamycin-resistance gene from Pseudomonas fluorescens R8 Tn5 pho mutant M1 (Williams and Fletcher 1996) grown in LB media supplemented with 50 µg ml^{-1} kanamycin, as previously described (Caton et al. 2004b). Real-time PCR reactions (annealing at 63 °C) contained a known quantity of the kanamycin gene, aliquots (2 µl) of extracts, and the primers KanR: 5′–GCTGACGGAATTTATGCCTCTTC–3′; positions 572-594 and KanF: 5′–CACCATGAGTGACGACTGAATCC–3′; positions 224-246.

</page>

<page number="4">

Inhibition of PCR amplification was less than 2%, compared to control reactions with no added extract.

NifH Clone Libraries and Cladistics

NifH clone libraries were generated using a TOPO-TA blue-white cloning system in E. coli (Invitrogen). Ten separate amplicon populations were purified by band excision from a 2% agarose gels and pooled for each sample. Clones (~200) were randomly collected and inoculated into 96-well plates. Plasmid isolation and insert sequencing was performed by a commercial vendor (Agencourt) using the UNIFF19F/NifDN primer set. Sequences were trimmed to remove remaining vector regions, leaving reads of 191-278 bp for analysis. The 125 reliable sequences obtained were too short for inclusion as a group in GenBank, but are available from the permanent SOAR repository at Wichita State University (https://soar.wichita.edu/handle/10057/14382).

Sequences were aligned using Clustal-W and trimmed in MacClade v4.08 (Sinauer Associates). Contextual 16S rRNA gene sequences were identified in GenBank using BLAST or by comparison to relevant literature (Ueda et al. 1995). Sequences were trimmed to equal lengths and positions with gaps and ambiguous bases were ignored, giving 191 positions for analysis. PAUP 4.0 b10 generated phylogenetic trees using distance analysis with Jukes-Cantor rules and the neighbor-joining algorithm. The tree was rooted using the sequence from Methanocaldococcus jannaschii as the functional outgroup. The diversity of nifH genes and species assignments between and within the three stream types were compared using MEGA7 (Kumar et al. 2016), the Biodiversity Assessment Tools (BAT) package function beta.multi within R (Cardoso et al. 2014), and log-likelihood ratio tests using the \( G \) statistic and two-sample ranking with the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test (Zar 2009).

Results

Rates of Nitrogen Fixation

The results of N\(_2\) fixation assays are presented in Table 3 for stream sediment samples taken from three locations along each of six prairie stream reaches. The highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation in stream sediments were observed at locations on two reaches of Kings Creek, the least impacted stream, having the lowest nitrate levels in our study (Table 3). Although it is considered an agricultural stream, Natalie’s Creek had nitrate levels as low as the pristine stream Kings Creek at the time of sampling; however, it did not exhibit high N\(_2\)-fixation rates in sediments. The North Creek agricultural stream sediment had somewhat elevated nitrate levels and a high rate of N\(_2\) fixation was observed in some sediment samples. The lowest rates of N\(_2\) fixation were observed in the urban stream sediments and these corresponded to the greatest chronic nitrate loads. It should be noted that acetylene reduction assays are surrogates for N fixation and a common conversion factor (3.8) was used here for calculations (Jensen and Cox 1983). While this allows for comparison within these data, actual values for N fixation would be altered if this ratio were to differ substantially between samples. Stable isotope methods would give a direct measure of N fixation activity that could be used to determine if any samples deviated from the common ratio used for

</page>

<page number="5">

conversion, however, the accepted range is 3 to 4 (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Zehr and Montoya 2007).

The rates of N_2 fixation across our six prairie streams varied between 1.6 and 28.0 fmol g^{-1} h^{-1}. The highest rates were observed in pristine prairie streams and the lowest rates were observed in urban stream sediments (Fig. 1). Log-transformed rates and concentrations (n = 6, fd = 4) were used for statistical analyses using Pearson correlations. N_2-fixation rates were significantly negatively correlated (r = -0.811, p = 0.050) with the extent of chronic N loading of the streams, as measured by NO_3^- levels in sediments. In a similar fashion, DIN levels in the streams were negatively correlated with N_2-fixation activity in sediments, with marginal statistical significance (r = -0.745, p = 0.089) (Fig. 2). This is expected since nearly all of the DIN was due to NO_3^- (Table 2), with NO_3^- and DIN levels significantly positively correlated (r = 0.969, p = 0.001). Rates of N_2 fixation were not correlated with NH_4-N (r = -0.181, p = 0.731) or with DON (r = 0.691, p = 0.196).

Overall rates of denitrification were low and varied from undetectable to 44.0 μg N m^{-2} s^{-1} (Fig. 3). Denitrification rates in sediments were significantly negatively correlated with N_2-fixation activity (r = -0.809, p = 0.050). The rates of nitrification were not significantly correlated to the rates of N_2 fixation (r = -0.616, p = 0.193), nor were NO_3^- fluxes (r = -0.548, p = 0.260).

Significant correlations were not observed between N_2-fixation rates and PAR (r = -0.334, p = 0.517) or GPP (r = 0.331, p = 0.522). No significant correlation (r = 0.446, p = 0.376) was found between N_2-fixation rates and DO either. The width (r = 0.047, p = 0.929) or depth (r = 0.125, p = 0.814) of the streams did not significantly correlate with N_2-fixation rates. A marginally significant negative correlation (r = -0.799, p = 0.057) was observed between temperature and N_2-fixation rates across our six streams. Stream type significantly correlated (r = 0.923, p = 0.009) with N_2-fixation rates as expected, since the streams had different levels of chronic N loading.

In addition to regular sediment sampling along each reach, targeted grab samples were taken of leaf litter and algal mats along these reaches (Table 4). Rates of N_2 fixation in these targeted grab samples were generally higher than in sediment samples. Leaf litter samples from Kings Creek exhibited high rates of N_2 fixation in the N4D reach. Natalie’s Creek had algal mats along its banks and these exhibited very high rates of N_2 fixation. Similarly, the algal materials from the Big Blue River Ditch also exhibited high rates of N_2 fixation. The Big Blue River Ditch is canalized in this region and the algal samples were taken from depressions in the concrete and from algal streamers.

Levels of *NifH* Genes

Direct DNA extracts were made from field-frozen sediment samples taken at the same locations as those assayed for N_2-fixation activity. The greatest overall abundance of *nifH* genes was observed in the sediments from Kings Creek, with all samples above 10^4 copies g^{-1} (Table 3). Campus Creek, an urban stream, had relatively high *nifH* abundance overall. One sample from Natalie’s Creek also showed high *nifH* abundance. The abundance of bacterial 16S rRNA genes varied from 10^8 to 10^{11} copies g^{-1} sediment. There was a

</page>

<page number="6">

significant correlation (r = 0.941, \( p = 0.005 \)) between stream type and bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance, but there was not a significant correlation (r = 0.588, \( p = 0.219 \)) between stream type and \( nifH \) gene abundance. Chronic NO\(_3^-\) loads were marginally correlated with bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance (r = 0.756, \( p = 0.082 \)), while \( nifH \) gene abundance was not (r = 0.472, \( p = 0.345 \)).

There was not a direct correlation between \( nifH \) gene abundance and N\(_2\)-fixation rates (r = 0.295, \( p = 0.570 \)) when comparing six stream averages or when comparing data for each reach (n = 17, r = 0.381, \( p = 0.131 \)). The abundance of bacterial 16S rRNA genes was positively correlated (r = 0.830, \( p = 0.041 \)) with N\(_2\)-fixation rates, while \( nifH \) gene abundance was only marginally correlated (r = 0.704, \( p = 0.118 \)) with N\(_2\)-fixation rates. No significant correlations were found between \( nifH \) or bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundances with DON, DIN, width, depth, PAR, GPP, DO, nitrate flux, denitrification, or nitrification. NH\(_4\)-N negatively correlates (r = 0.970, \( p = 0.006 \)) with \( nifH \) gene abundance, but not bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance (r = 0.485, \( p = 0.407 \)). There was a significant negative correlation between stream temperature and both \( nifH \) gene abundance (r = 0.869, \( p = 0.025 \)) and bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance (r = 0.899, \( p = 0.015 \)).

Targeted grab samples of leaf litter and algal mats mainly gave high abundances of \( nifH \) genes (Table 4), similar to the highest values obtained from sediment samples. Small sample size from the canalized concrete bed of Big Blue River Ditch may have led to the low values obtained from two small samples there. No significant correlations were observed between N\(_2\)-fixation rates, stream type, and \( nifH \) gene abundance for the grab samples. While the highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation generally were observed in grab samples, this was not correlated with \( nifH \) gene abundances.

**NifH Gene Clone Libraries**

Clone libraries were made from pooled PCR amplicons derived from metagenomic extracts of stream sediment samples. Clones of \( nifH \) genes from each of these libraries (125 total clones sequenced) were compared, along with contextual sequences, to generate the summary phylogenetic tree shown in Fig. 4. A complete tree is presented in supporting materials (Fig. S1). *NifH* genes from members of the *Deltaproteobacteria* were detected in the sediments of all three stream types, as were *nifH* genes from *Bradyrhizobium, Methylomonas, Rhizobium*, and *Sinorhizobium*. Cyanobacterial *nifH* sequences were observed in the agricultural and urban streams, although sediments and not algal mats were sampled. Quite a number of groups of *nifH* sequences that only cluster with sequences from uncultured organisms were observed in each of the streams. These include clones from grass, oil field, and rice soils, Mangrove rhizosphere, and marine environments. The larger cluster near *Bradyrhizobium japonicum* did not have strong matches to known sequences. No sequences related to *Archaea, Azotobacter, Chlorobium, Klebsiella*, or *Rhodobacter* were detected.

Taxonomic assignments were made from *nifH* sequences and compared across streams, showing obvious differences in guild composition. For example, *Methylococcus* sequences were only observed in the agricultural stream and sequences related to an uncultured Mangrove soil *nifH* were found in high abundance only in the urban stream. When isolates

</page>

<page number="7">

are binned at higher taxonomic levels (Cyanobacteria, *Deltaproteobacteria*, Others, Rhizobia, and Unknowns) the *G* statistic can be applied. Diazotroph communities among streams significantly differed by stream type by this measure (fd = 4, *p* <0.001). Whether binning *nifH* taxons by clade or higher levels, Wilcoxon rank sum analysis supported the hypothesis that diazotroph guild composition varies significantly with stream type (n = 5 to 14, *p* <0.01 to <0.001). When *nifH* sequences were examined directly, without assigning taxon and making common evolutionary assumptions (Jukes-Cantor rules), the results were quite different (Table 5). Within-group and between-group mean genetic distances were similar and generally high (>1). Net between group mean distances were low, taken together, indicating that diversity within each group was similar to diversity between the groups. This was supported by beta diversity analyses using Jaccard coefficients where values were consistently high (approaching 1) and were insensitive to randomization between groups. The coefficient of differentiation was very low (0.089 on a scale of 0 to 1), suggesting that the populations of *nifH* genes among the streams have similarities because there is substantial gene flow between these communities.

Discussion

The overall rates of N$_2$ fixation observed for prairie stream sediments in the current report are of the same magnitude as fixation rates from previous studies of small streams (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Leland and Carter 1985; Francis et al. 1985, Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2007). The metanalysis of Marcarelli et al. (2008) reported that the mean N$_2$-fixation rate among 22 streams was approximately 1 µmol N fixed m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$, with a high of 30 µmol N fixed m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$. Nitrogen-fixation activity in the stream sediments of our study ranged from about 0.1 to 3.0 µmol N fixed m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$. Rates of N$_2$ fixation were higher in grab samples suggesting that leaf litter and algal biofilms are important contributors to whole-stream N$_2$-fixation activity.

There was a significant correlation between N$_2$-fixation rates and levels of chronic N loading in these small streams (as NO$_3^-$ or DIN). It is well known that nitrate can inhibit N$_2$-fixation activity and this also has been observed in streams (Capone and Carpenter 1982; Grimm 1994). However, in brackish marshes, N$_2$ fixation proceeded even with the addition of fixed N compounds (Piceno and Lovell 2000). Controls on the rate of N$_2$ fixation appear more complicated than simply a response to NO$_3^-$ levels. Temperature was found to be correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates in our streams, as observed previously (Horne and Carmiggelt 1975; Grimm and Petrone 1997). Light and productivity (PAR and GPP) however were not correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates. Phosphorus levels were not measured as part of the LINXII project. Denitrification rates were significantly correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates. This was expected since denitrification rates also appear to vary with nitrate levels (Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2006, 2007), although this correlation was not strong in the current study (r = 0.695, *p* = 0.126).

The rates of NO$_3^-$ uptake in our streams ranged from 0.24 to 15.4 mg N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$, in North Creek and Campus Creek, respectively (O’Brien et al. 2007). Highly impacted urban streams exhibited uptake rates of >5 mg N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$, while pristine and agricultural streams exhibited uptake rates of \( \leq 1 \) mg N m$^{-2}$ h$^{-1}$. While NO$_3^-$ uptake rates were higher than N$_2$-

</page>

<page number="8">

fixation rates for all streams, those with lower uptake rates tended to have higher fixation rates (r = 0.685, \( p = 0.133 \)). For the pristine prairie stream Kings K2A, the rate of N\(_2\) fixation is about 15% of the NO\(_3^-\) uptake rate (on an areal basis). This suggests that N\(_2\) fixation can be a significant contributor to stream N budgets. However, for our other pristine prairie stream Kings N4D, the N\(_2\)-fixation rate was only 2% of the NO\(_3^-\) uptake rate. None of the other streams had N\(_2\)-fixation rates that were more than 6% of their NO\(_3^-\) uptake rates, with the Big Blue Ditch value being only 0.02%. Taken together, this suggests that the impact of N\(_2\) fixation to the N budget of small streams is variable. While N\(_2\) fixation may be a substantial contributor in streams with low chronic N loads, this does not appear to be consistent, and N\(_2\) fixation does not seem to be a substantial contributor to N budgets in small streams with higher chronic N loads. This is in agreement with previous studies, both in terms of the variability observed across streams, but also in concluding that N\(_2\) fixation can be important in certain oligotrophic streams and perhaps only at certain times (Marcarelli and Wurtsbaugh 2007; Marcarelli et al. 2008; Scott et al. 2009; Lang et al. 2012; Kunza and Hall 2013, 2014).

Patchiness is a key feature of small streams, in terms of leaf litter and algal mat distributions, and this reflects differences in N\(_2\)-fixation rates across stream compartments. The highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation are often associated with patches of leaf litter and algal mats, and the current study agrees (Henry and Fisher 2003; Marcarelli et al. 2008). Targeted grab samples in our study exhibited the highest rates of N\(_2\) fixation, substantially higher than equivalent amounts of sediments. To better understand the role of N\(_2\) fixation in stream N budgets, coverage estimates for algal mats and leaf litter are needed, but this was not done rigorously in the current study. No significant correlations were observed between N\(_2\)-fixation rates and estimates of fine benthic organic matter or ash-free dry mass (g dry mass m\(^{-2}\)) of leaves, wood, and epilithon (estimates from O’Brien et al. 2007). Samples of algal mats exhibited N\(_2\)-fixation rates some 30-fold greater than in the bottom sediments. Thus, even if only 3% of a basin was covered with algal mats, their contribution to N\(_2\) fixation might equal that of the remaining 97% of the basin comprised of sediments.

At Kings Creek N4D, patches of leaf litter were found to have N\(_2\)-fixation rates that were 4-fold greater than the sediments of this reach. This stream has a cobbled bottom with limited areas of sediment. Seasonal factors and scouring events will have a role in determining the balance between fixation in sediments and leaf litter in streams like Kings Creek. Finally, the concrete basin of Big Blue River Ditch had remarkably productive patches. N\(_2\)-fixation activity was high in algal communities within depressions and grooves in the concrete and in algal streamers attached to the bottom. The patchiness of organisms actively fixing N make whole-stream assessments more difficult especially since the patches are often transient and subject to changes in stream flow, seasons, and nutrient inputs.

The contribution of N\(_2\) fixation to stream N budgets may be more significant in specific patches of streams or in certain streams. Diazotrophs may have a selective advantage in streams with low N loading. The same may be true for microniches where fixed N could be locally limiting, even in bulk sediments that do not appear to be N-limited. Channeling of fixed N compounds from cyanobacteria to attendant bacterial communities is well known (Scott and Marcarelli 2012). The coupling of diazotrophs to symbiotic bacteria (and fungi)

</page>

<page number="9">

can affect microbial community structure more broadly and may influence stream geochemical processes beyond N$_2$ fixation and assimilation (Tank and Dodds 2003; O’Brien et al. 2007).

While correlations emerged between the rates of N cycle processes in our study, few statistically significant correlations were observed between process-level measurements and the abundance of *nifH* genes, with the exception of temperature and NH$_4$-N levels. There was a strong positive correlation of temperature with both *nifH* and bacterial 16S rRNA gene abundance. The abundance of *nifH* genes was not significantly correlated with N$_2$-fixation rates. An explanation for the weakness of the correlation between *nifH* gene abundance and N$_2$-fixation rates is that *nifH* gene copy number simply does not reflect the activity of the gene. Examination of *nifH* transcripts would provide more insight. Diazotrophs are known with more than one copy of their *nifH* genes, which could skew ratios (Ueda et al. 1995; Zehr et al. 1997). Seasonal changes, disturbances, and changing inputs may encourage a flexible stable guild. It also is possible that the N pollution in these streams has not persisted for long enough to change the abundance and distribution of microbes in the N$_2$-fixing guild. While the abundance of bacterial 16S rRNA genes significantly correlated with stream type, the abundance of *nifH* genes did not. Further, there were no significant correlations between the abundance of *nifH* genes and levels of chronic nitrate loading.

We recovered a number of *nifH* gene sequences from sediment clone libraries that mainly clustered with oligotrophic taxa associated with diazotrophy in soils. There were sequences from *Deltaproteobacteria* in all stream types for instance. A variety of Rhizobia were detected, but no sequences from *Azotobacter* or *Klebsiella*. While the *nifH* primers were capable of amplifying genes from *Archaea, Chlorobium, Rhodobacter* and these others, no corresponding sequences were detected. Cyanobacterial *nifH* gene sequences were recovered from sediments and would presumably be abundant in diazotrophic algal mats. Biodiversity estimates based on *nifH* sequence libraries indicated that there were similar diazotroph guilds across stream type, maintained by substantial gene flow between communities. However, there are significant differences between the diazotroph guilds among stream types when taxa are examined. There are likely to be other microbial contributors to N$_2$ fixation in stream sediments, which could be uncovered with more robust sequencing campaigns.

Seasonal variation and cross-shelf distribution of the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium, in southern East China Sea Jeng Chang a,*, Kuo-Ping Chiang b, Gwo-Ching Gong c a Institute of Marine Biology, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC b Department of Fishery Science, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC c Department of Oceanography, National Taiwan Ocean University, Keelung 202-24, Taiwan, ROC Abstract The abundance of a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium, in the southern East China Sea was surveyed along a cross-shelf transect from 1993 to 1996. Trichodesmium existed mostly in surface water between 0 and 50 m depth, with population densities ranging from 0 to 600 trichomes l\(^{-1}\). A clear seasonal cycle was observed in Trichodesmium standing crop which reached more than 10\(^7\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) in summer and became undetectable in winter. The cross-shelf distribution showed a spring-type pattern with higher abundance in the Kuroshio current and low abundance in the coastal zone. In fall months, a reversed distribution pattern appeared with high abundance in the coastal zone and decreasing concentrations toward the shelf break. These distribution patterns were difficult to be explained by temperature alone, and a coastal substance may be important in determining Trichodesmium distribution in shelf seas. The calculated nitrogen fixation rate of Trichodesmium ranged from 0.1 to 59 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) in the upwelling zone and Kuroshio under non-bloom conditions. This result suggested that Trichodesmium is one of the major contributors to new production in Kuroshio waters. Keywords: Cyanobacterium; East China Sea; Nitrogen fixation; Trichodesmium abundance 1. Introduction Trichodesmium is a filamentous cyanobacterium that inhabits tropical and subtropical seas (for a recent review, see Capone et al., 1997). Trichodesmium is also diazotrophic, a term which depicts its ability to produce ammonium from dinitrogen, and nitrogen fixed via this process supports a significant amount of new production globally (Karl et al., 1997). For example, in the tropical North Atlantic Ocean, Trichodesmium has been shown as the most important new nitrogen source in the euphotic zone (Carpenter and Romans, 1991). At a station in North Pacific Ocean near Hawaii, Trichodesmium supports 27% of the new production under non-bloom conditions (Letelier and Karl, 1996). On the other hand, the importance of Trichodesmium and nitrogen fixation to nutrient dynamics in shelf seas is less clear. According to Trichodesmium abundance and nitrogen fixation rates measured in East China Sea, Saino and Hattori (1980) estimated that 6% of the nitrogen requirement in supporting annual primary production was provided by this cyanobacterium. In addition, shelf seas may receive biologically fixed nitrogen originated from the open ocean. Based on \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) measurements, Liu et al. (1996) estimated that 20% of the nitrate supplied by an upwelling system, which pumped Kuroshio subsurface water to East China Sea, came from nitrogen fixation. An understanding of the distribution of diazotrophic organisms in shelf seas is important to the modeling of nitrogen fixation as well as carbon cycling in these ecosystems. Equipped with buoyancy-regulating gas vesicles and nitrogen fixation enzymes, Trichodesmium is regarded as an organism well adapted to stratified, oligotrophic conditions (Capone et al., 1997). Thus, Trichodesmium abundance should be high in the boundary current and decrease toward the coast as nitrogenous nutrients become more available. Although such a pattern has been regularly observed in the East China Sea during summer months (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974), other distribution patterns do exist. Data presented by Marumo and Asaoka (1974) during one summer cruise revealed a second maximum of Trichodesmium abundance near the coast. In addition, the frequently occurring coastal blooms of this cyanobacterium suggested that it can survive and compete with other phytoplankton in coastal waters (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974; Hong et al., 1992). The interest in studying Trichodesmium distribution also comes from recent reports about harmful blooms of this organism which caused damages to local fish and shellfish populations (Hong et al., 1992). The adverse effects of blooms may be related to several toxins generated by Trichodesmium which are lethal to marine organisms including copepods and mackerel fish (Hawser et al., 1992; Endean et al., 1993). The recognition of environmental conditions that favor bloom formation thus has social and economical implications. In this report, Trichodesmium abundance obtained from 12 cruises along a cross-shelf cruise track in southern East China Sea was analyzed in the hope of understanding spatial and temporal distributions of this organism in shelf seas. From the observed distribution patterns, possible controlling mechanisms were inferred, and estimates were made for the amount of nitrogen fixed by Trichodesmium. 2. Materials and methods A total of 12 cruises were conducted between November 1993 and April 1996 to collect water samples for Trichodesmium enumeration in the southern East China Sea Table 1 Research cruises during which water samples have been collected for the enumeration of Trichodesmium abundance. During each cruise, stations visited in the coastal zone (C), the mid-shelf zone (M), the upwelling zone (U), and the Kuroshio zone (K) are listed separately

aOR I: Ocean Researcher I; OR II: Ocean Researcher II. bSailing along the KEEPKEY transect. ![Map of the study area and locations of sampling stations](page_1012_1342_670_377.png) Fig. 1. Map of the study area and locations of sampling stations. Filled circles (●) indicate KEEPKEY stations with the odd-numbered stations labeled. Stations off the KEEPKEY transect were visited during the April 1995 (○), the January 1996 (▲), and the April 1996 cruises (△), respectively. Names of the four hydrographic zones used in the text are marked above the corresponding stations. (Table 1). All cruise tracks ran in a cross-shelf direction and were approximately normal to isobaths (Fig. 1). Among them, eight cruises sailed along a transect starting at 26°20′N, 120°30′E and ending at 25°0′N, 123°10′E, and the other four cruises visited stations in the close vicinity. The major transect was named KEEPKEY transect since it has been frequently surveyed during the operation period of the KEEP (Kuroshio Edge Exchange Processes) project. The hydrography along the KEEPKEY transect is fairly well known and several zones can be recognized according to physical and chemical properties of sea water (Gong et al., 1995, 1996). The region between KEEPKEY stations 1 and 3 is the coastal zone, and is typically occupied by the low temperature, low salinity coastal water. Stations 5 and 7 belong to the mid-shelf zone occupied by low nutrient Taiwan Strait water, and stations 9 to 11 are usually occupied by high nutrient water from an upwelling system. The region between stations 15 and 17 is the Kuroshio zone. The euphotic zone in this region is always occupied by warm, nutrient-poor Kuroshio water (Fig. 1). Water samples for Trichodesmium enumeration were collected with a rosette sampler equipped with 2.5 l Go-Flo bottles (General Oceanics, Miami). One liter of sea water was transferred to plastic bottles and fixed immediately with acidic Lugol’s solution (Thronsdon, 1978). In the laboratory, phytoplankton cells in water samples were allowed to settle for at least 48 h and the supernatant was carefully withdrawn by an aspirator until about 50 ml remained in the bottle. The concentrated water sample was then transferred to a conical centrifuge tube and stored in dark at 4°C. Immediately before microscope examination, the sample was concentrated again to a final volume of 1 ml, and loaded to a Sedgwick–Rafter counting cell. The entire counting cell was scanned using a Nikon Optiphot-2 microscope at 100×, and number of trichomes (Trichodesmium filaments) encountered were used to evaluate Trichodesmium abundance. A small fraction of trichomes in our sample were less than 200 μm in length. These short trichomes were excluded in our counts to avoid bias. According to our preliminary experiment (Chang, 1999), Trichodesmium abundance generated this way showed no significant difference from filtering 1 l of sea water onto a Nuclepore filter on deck followed by epi-fluorescent microscope counting. Counting 10 samples repeatedly collected from the same depth at a station revealed that a single-sample estimate should carry a coefficient of variation of 62%. As a result, the present counting method was intended for the detection of abundance differences greater than an order of magnitude. A somewhat different method was adopted to count trichomes in samples from the July cruise in 1994. Samples were settled in 100 ml Utermöhl sedimentation cylinders and counted on a Nikon inverted-microscope (Hasle, 1978). Samples from the KEEPKEY station 1 of the May 1994 cruise have been counted by the Sedgwick–Rafter method and the Utermöhl method, and both methods did not detect any trichomes in the water column. An examination of the abundance of a chain-forming diatom, Rhizosolenia, in the same batch of samples revealed that the difference between these two counting methods ranged from 0 to 200%. Temperature and salinity data were measured with a Seabird CTD (SBE9/11 plus, Seabird Inc. WA). The mixed layer depth was obtained from the upper region on a density profile where the variation in \( \sigma_0 \) was less than 0.16. Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were measured in duplicates using a Turner Designs Fluorometer (Model 10-AU-005) according to standard procedures (Parsons et al., 1984). Samples for nutrient determination were quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen and then stored at \( -18^\circ \mathrm{C} \) until analysis. The concentration of nitrate and nitrite were determined by the pink azo dye method, and phosphate were determined by the molybdenum blue method (Parsons et al., 1984; Pai et al., 1990; Gong, 1992). 3. Results In all samples, Trichodesmium mainly appeared as individual trichomes. Colonial forms existed, but were very rare. As a result, attempts were not made to distinguish between various species in this genus. Of all stations visited, Trichodesmium trichomes always existed in the surface layer (Figs. 2(a) and 3(a)). Population densities decreased rapidly when depth became greater than 50 m. A maximum of biomass usually occurred at a depth of 20–30 m. Sometimes, a second maximum appeared near sea surface (Fig. 3(a)). In the Kuroshio, the highest abundance occurred in May 1995, reaching 276 trichomes l\(^{-1}\) at KEEPKEY station 17 (Fig. 2(a)). The abundance was greatly reduced in winter months. At most a few trichomes were found in a liter of sea water. The depth-integrated Trichodesmium abundance showed a clear seasonal cycle with March to May as the growth phase and September to November as the decline phase (Fig. 2(b)). However, the year-to-year variation in Trichodesmium standing crop can not be overlooked. For example, in May 1995, \(10^7\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) was observed in Kuroshio. In contrast, only \(10^5\) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) was observed at the end of April 1996, a reduction of 100 times (Fig. 2(b)). Environmental factors in Kuroshio possessed a similar seasonal cycle. Water temperature was 24\(^\circ\)C in winter, but increased to 29\(^\circ\)C in summer (Fig. 2(c)). As for mixing strength, strong northeast monsoons in winter generated a mixed layer more than 100 m thick. When weather became more stable in summer, the mixed layer depths were typically around 30 m. The seasonal variation of Trichodesmium standing crop in the upwelling region had a pattern resembling that in the Kuroshio with higher abundance in summer (Fig. 3(b)). The highest population density observed was 600 trichomes l\(^{-1}\). Compared to the seasonal cycle in the Kuroshio, Trichodesmium declined earlier in the upwelling region. Starting from the end of September, no trichomes were detected in this area. The cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium revealed different patterns in spring, summer, and fall. In spring, cold water with temperature around 20\(^\circ\)C occupied the area between the coast and the upwelling while Kuroshio water was still warmer than 24\(^\circ\)C (Fig. 4(a)). On the four cruises that covered the KEEPKEY transect in spring months, Trichodesmium was always undetectable in the coastal zone (Fig. 5(a)). However, at a distance of 150–250 km from shore, trichomes started to appear, and population densities increased toward Kuroshio. In contrast, phytoplankton biomass, as indicated by chlorophyll \(a\) concentrations, was constantly low in the Kuroshio (Fig. 4(d)). High levels of chlorophyll were usually observed at the outer fringe of the upwelling, apparently supported by the nutrients supplied from the deep (Figs. 4(b) and (c)). In fall, the difference in temperature between Kuroshio and coastal water was less than 3\(^\circ\) (Fig. 4(a)). A sudden drop near stations 11 to 13 marked the presence of cold Fig. 2. Trichodesmium vertical distribution and seasonal variation in the Kuroshio zone. (a) Representative abundance profiles observed in various seasons. (b) Seasonal variation of depth integrated abundance. The depth of integration was 50 m for KEEPKEY stations 1 to 5, and 70 m for stations 6 to 17, respectively. Various symbols are used to distinguish data collected from 1993 (○), 1994 (●), 1995 (▽), and 1996 (▼). The symbol marked by an arrow indicates that the actual value of that data point was 0 trichome m^{-2}. (c) Seasonal variation of temperature (■) and mixing depth (□) in Kuroshio. Water temperature were measured at 10 m depth. Curves are polynomial regression lines to indicate the general trend. water in the upwelling, and coincided with high concentrations of nutrients (Figs. 4(b) and (c)). Compared to the distribution of Trichodesmium in spring, a completely reversed pattern appeared in fall. Based on available data from two cruises in 1993 and 1995, Trichodesmium standing crop reached 1.6–3.2 \times 10^6 trichomes m^{-2} in the Fig. 3. Trichodesmium vertical distribution and seasonal variation in the upwelling zone. (a) Representative abundance profiles observed in various seasons. (b) Seasonal variation of depth integrated abundance. Symbols are the same as in Fig. 2(b), and the curve is a polynomial regression line to indicate the general trend. coastal zone but was virtually undetectable in the upwelling zone and Kuroshio (Fig. 5(b)). Relatively few data sets were obtained in summer. In July of 1994, a segment of the KEEPKEY transect on the outer shelf was surveyed, and water temperature was constantly warmer than 28°C (Fig. 4(a)). Trichodesmium abundance ranged from \( 5.7 \times 10^6 \) to \( 1.3 \times 10^7 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) with a mean trichome length of 107 cells. Substantial variation was observed between stations which indicated a patchy distribution (Fig. 5(b)). Such high abundance apparently did not occur in every summer. When KEEPKEY station 8 was visited in July 1995, the integrated abundance of Trichodesmium was merely \( 2.7 \times 10^4 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\). 4. Discussion Our results indicated that the cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium changed annually with seasons (Fig. 5). The spring-type distribution with higher abundance in Fig. 4. Typical cross-shelf variation in seawater properties observed in spring (△, April 1996 cruise), summer (○, July 1994 cruise), and fall (●, October 1995 cruise). (a) Temperature measured at 10 m depth. (b) Depth integrated nitrate and nitrite concentration. The integration depth is the same as in Fig. 2. (c) Depth integrated phosphate concentration. (d) Phytoplankton standing stock expressed as chlorophyll \( a \) concentration. Kuroshio agreed well with patterns previously observed in the East China Sea (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974). The fall-type distribution with higher abundance in the coastal zone received less attention before, but other independent observations supported the existence of such a pattern. A survey in Taiwan Strait indicated that Trichodesmium reached annual maximum in September with the highest abundance at \( 2 \times 10^3 \) trichomes l\(^{-1}\) found near the mainland coast (Fujian Institute of Oceanology, (a) Spring ![Cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium in spring](page_370_312_670_370.png) (b) Summer (○) and Fall (△ ●) ![Cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium in summer and fall](page_370_740_670_670.png) Fig. 5. The cross-shelf distributions of Trichodesmium abundance observed in (a) spring and (b) summer and fall. The cruises were conducted in May 1994 (◇), March 1995 (▼), April 1995 (◆), April 1996 (▽), July 1994 (○), November 1993 (△), and October 1995 (●). 1988). In addition, all Trichodesmium blooms reported were very close to coast, and all occurred in summer and fall (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974; Hong et al., 1992). Temperature has long been recognized as a major factor that controls Trichodesmium abundance, and 20°C was considered as the minimum temperature for Trichodesmium to survive (Marumo and Nagasawa, 1976; Carpenter, 1983a). In spring, the scarcity of Trichodesmium in the coastal zone was apparently a result of poor growth due to the less than 20°C temperature (Figs. 4 and 5). As the temperature (a) Spring ![Scatter plot showing log (abundance+1) vs Temperature (°C) for spring distribution](page_324_312_1012_384.png) (b) Fall ![Scatter plot showing log (abundance+1) vs Temperature (°C) for fall distribution](page_324_748_1012_384.png) Fig. 6. The cross-shelf distribution of Trichodesmium explained by the variation in water temperature. (a) Spring distribution and temperature. Symbols are the same as in Fig. 5, and temperature was measured at 10 m depth. The straight line marks a significant regression relationship: \( \log (A + 1) = -0.401 + 0.252\ T \) (\( P < 0.05, r = 0.56 \)), where \( A \) is the integrated Trichodesmium abundance (trichomes m\(^{-2}\)), and \( T \) is temperature. All non-zero data from the four spring cruises were included in the regression. (b) Fall distribution and temperature. The regression generated nonsignificant result. Symbols are the same as in Fig. 5. increased toward the Kuroshio, Trichodesmium became more abundant. When spring data between 1994 and 1996 were combined, a statistically significant relationship was found between temperature at 10 m depth and integrated Trichodesmium abundance (Fig. 6(a)). The positive correlation existed even when data points with zero value were excluded from the regression. However, temperature alone was unable to explain all distribution patterns observed in the East China Sea. For the fall-type distribution, no relationship with water temperature could be established (Fig. 6(b)). The population density in the Kuroshio was 30 times less than that in the coastal zone while water temperature in Kuroshio remained warmer than 28°C (Figs. 4 and 5). Similarly, temperature alone failed to explain the observed seasonal cycle of Trichodesmium in Kuroshio (Fig. 2). The Kuroshio water near Taiwan is constantly warmer than 24°C year-round. Thus, it is surprising to see that Trichodesmium abundance went through such an dramatic change in a year. Of course, *Trichodesmium*'s ability in fixing nitrogen is vulnerable to turbulence (Carpenter and Price, 1976), and the strong mixing in winter might cause *Trichodesmium* abundance to decrease in the warm Kuroshio (Fig. 2(c)). However, a rapid decrease in *Trichodesmium* abundance was noticed in fall when water temperature was still high and the mixing depth was shallower than 50 m (Fig. 2). Marumo and Asaoka (1974) proposed that a substance in coastal water is essential for the growth of *Trichodesmium*. Because of this substance, dense *Trichodesmium* populations formed at several locations along the course of Kuroshio where the mixing with coastal waters took place (Marumo and Asaoka, 1974). In our study area, the most intensive mixing between the coastal water and the Kuroshio current occurs in winter when part of the Kuroshio flows onto the East China Sea continental shelf (Gong et al., 1997). As a result, ample amount of this substance enters the Kuroshio zone during winter, and supports *Trichodesmium* growth in spring when mixing depth decreases. Later, the active growth in spring and summer deprived this substance from Kuroshio which in turn retarded *Trichodesmium* growth and caused the standing crop to shrink in fall (Figs. 2 and 4). Meanwhile, temperature in the coastal zone was quite warm in fall, and a continuous supply of this substance stimulated the growth of *Trichodesmium*, caused its biomass to increase, and created an environment favoring bloom formation. The phenomenon of a coastal substance in controlling *Trichodesmium* distribution was further supported by observations made on a cruise that covered the entire East China Sea in 1992. High trichome concentrations were mainly found in an area influenced by the Yangtze River (Chen et al., 1996; Gong et al., 1996). However, there is no direct evidence to confirm such a relationship in East China Sea, and other mechanisms, such as the grazing by toxin-resistant harpacticoid copepods (O’Neil and Roman, 1994), cannot be excluded as possible causes for the observed distribution patterns. The amount of new nitrogen introduced to East China Sea and Kuroshio by *Trichodesmium* can be estimated from trichome concentration and nitrogen fixation rate. According to measurements conducted in Kuroshio near southern Japan (Saino and Hattori, 1980), an averaged acetylene reduction rate was 0.7 pmole ethylene trichome\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\) in samples containing only individual trichomes. If we accept the theoretical 3 : 1 acetylene reduction to nitrogen fixation conversion ratio (Capone, 1993), and the fact that *Trichodesmium* fixes nitrogen only in sunlight hours (assumed to be 12 h per day, Saino and Hattori, 1980), nitrogen fixation rate in the Kuroshio/East China Sea region would be 5.6 pmol N trichome\(^{-1}\) d\(^{-1}\). Based on *Trichodesmium* abundance observed at our study area, nitrogen fixation rate in Kuroshio was estimated as between 0.1 and 59 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) (Table 2). This estimate was extremely close to the 34 \( \pm \) 11 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) nitrogen fixation input required to maintain the depletion of \(^{15}\)N observed at 100 m depth in the same region (Liu et al., 1996). Using the same computational procedure, if *Trichodesmium* nitrogen fixation was not suppressed by the elevated nitrate supply in the upwelling region, the resultant nitrogen input would range from 0.3 to 34 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\) (Table 2). When the nitrogen fixation rate was converted to primary productivity using the Redfield ratio (C : N ratio by atoms = 106 : 16; Carpenter, 1983b), *Trichodesmium* Table 2 Estimated Trichodesmium nitrogen fixation rate and its contribution to primary production in southern East China Sea

Since the \( f \)-ratio in Kuroshio ranged from 0.09 to 0.25 (Gong, unpublished), Trichodesmium may contribute up to 25% of the local new production. In contrast, the fraction of primary production supported by nitrogen fixation in the upwelling zone was much less (Table 2). However, because Trichodesmium blooms were never encountered during our survey, the above estimate reflected nitrogen input under non-bloom conditions. Recent evidence indicated that nitrogen fixation rate in a Trichodesmium bloom can reach a very high level at 150 pg N trichome−1 h−1 (129 pmol N trichome−1 d−1), presumably due to colony formation (Carpenter and Capone, 1992). In August 1990, high densities of Trichodesmium at \( 3.7 \times 10^4 \) trichomes l−1 was observed at a station in the mid-shelf zone of East China Sea (Chen, 1992). If this bloom extended from sea surface to a depth of merely 1 m, the depth-integrated biomass would reach \( 3.7 \times 10^7 \) trichomes m−2. When the nitrogen fixation rate under bloom condition was applied, Trichodesmium would support a primary productivity of 31.5 mmol C m−2 d−1, much higher than total primary productivity normally measured in the Kuroshio zone. Since the \( f \)-ratio in Kuroshio ranged from 0.09 to 0.25 (Gong, unpublished), Trichodesmium may contribute up to 25% of the local new production. In contrast, the fraction of primary production supported by nitrogen fixation in the upwelling zone was much less (Table 2). However, because Trichodesmium blooms were never encountered during our survey, the above estimate reflected nitrogen input under non-bloom conditions. Recent evidence indicated that nitrogen fixation rate in a Trichodesmium bloom can reach a very high level at 150 pg N trichome−1 h−1 (129 pmol N trichome−1 d−1), presumably due to colony formation (Carpenter and Capone, 1992). In August 1990, high densities of Trichodesmium at \( 3.7 \times 10^4 \) trichomes l−1 was observed at a station in the mid-shelf zone of East China Sea (Chen, 1992). If this bloom extended from sea surface to a depth of merely 1 m, the depth-integrated biomass would reach \( 3.7 \times 10^7 \) trichomes m−2. When the nitrogen fixation rate under bloom condition was applied, Trichodesmium would support a primary productivity of 31.5 mmol C m−2 d−1, much higher than total primary productivity normally measured in the Kuroshio zone. Epiphytic Nitrogen Fixation Associated With Standing Dead Shoots of Smooth Cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora CAROLYN A. CURRIN1 National Marine Fisheries Service National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Beaufort Laboratory 101 Pivers Island Road Beaufort, North Carolina 28516 HANS W. PAERL University of North Carolina Institute of Marine Sciences Morehead City, North Carolina 28516 ABSTRACT: N_2 fixation associated with the epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora shoots was examined in both a natural and transplanted salt marsh in North Carolina. Acetylene reduction (AR) assays were conducted over a 24-mo period to estimate N_2 fixation rates on standing dead stems and leaves. In the natural salt marsh, mean AR rates ranged from 0.5 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 14 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, while in the transplanted marsh mean AR rates ranged from 1 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1} to 33 nmol C_2H_4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}. Diel AR activity of epiphytic communities in both marshes varied seasonally. Midday incubations yielded higher AR rates than nighttime incubations in the spring, while midday incubations in late summer and fall generally yielded AR rates equal to or lower than nighttime incubations. Desiccation during low tides occasionally repressed AR activity, although AR rates quickly rebounded with wetting. AR activity was localized in the epiphytic community, rather than in the underlying Spartina stem material. Based on the measured AR rates and the density of standing dead stems, the annual input of new N to the natural salt marsh via epiphytic N_2 fixation is estimated to be 2.6 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. The estimate of annual input of new N to the transplanted marsh is 3.8 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}. These estimates should be added to previous estimates of N_2 fixation in marsh sediments to estimate the total contribution of new nitrogen to salt marsh nitrogen budgets. Introduction Salt marsh primary production is often limited by the availability of fixed nitrogen (Valiela 1983). Accordingly, there have been numerous efforts to quantify the amount of new N added to salt marsh ecosystems via N_2 fixation (Valiela 1983; Capone 1985; Howarth et al. 1988). The majority of previous studies have focused on sedimentary N_2 fixation, including surface and subsurface sediments, and rhizospheric N_2 fixation associated with live Spartina alterniflora. Epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina stems and leaves has also been recorded (Green and Edmisten 1974; Hanson 1977; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981; Talbot et al. 1988; Newell et al. 1992). Of these studies, three provide estimates of the annual N input from epiphytic N_2 fixation, which vary by over two orders of magnitude. Two lower estimates are from Georgia and Louisiana salt marshes, where epiphytic N_2 fixation associated with Spartina leaves and stems was estimated to yield 0.47 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} and 0.66 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1}, respectively (Hanson 1977; Casselman et al. 1981). In a Florida salt marsh, epiphytic N_2 fixation was estimated to yield 287 g N m^{-2} yr^{-1} (Green and Edmisten 1974, but see Newell et al. 1992). The Louisiana and Georgia epiphytic communities were dominated by diatoms and eukaryotic, filamentous and coccoid algae. Cyanobacteria represented an average of 4% of the total epiphytic biovolume in Georgia (Fallon et al. 1985), and were absent from the Louisiana epiphytic community (Day et al. 1973). Two genera of N_2-fixing bacteria (Rhodospirillum and Rhodopseudomonas) were cultured from the epiphytic community examined in Florida, while cyanobacteria were only isolated from sediment samples (Green and Edmisten 1974). The epiphytic community on standing dead Spartina alterniflora in North Carolina salt marshes includes cyanobacteria (Calothrix spp. and Lyngbya spp. were dominant), diatoms, green algae, and heterotrophic and photosynthetic bacteria (Currin and Paerl 1997). Results from diel experiments suggest that N_2 fixation in this community is light-dependent, and that cyanobacteria are the microorganisms primarily responsible for the observed N_2-fixing activity. On an areal basis, estimated daily N_2 fixation rates (acetylene reduction assays) on standing dead Spartina stems were as high as 50 mg N m^{-2} d^{-1} (Currin and Paerl 1997), comparable to the highest rates recorded from other salt marsh environments (Capone 1983, 1985). Environmental factors controlling epiphytic N_2 fixation have been examined utilizing standing dead leaves and stems collected from Sapelo Island, Georgia (Newell et al. 1992). In that study, N_2 fixation rates as estimated by acetylene reduction (AR) assays were lowest during the winter on leaves with low ash content (<15%), while leaves collected May–August contained a higher ash content (>40%) and exhibited AR rates that were 10 times higher than the winter AR rates. Standing dead stems and leaves demonstrated similar AR rates on an ash-free dry weight (AFDW) basis. Newly senescent leaves had very low AR rates until 4 wk after tagging, and AR rates continued to rise throughout the 12-wk period after tagging. Other investigators have also documented higher rates of AR on dead stems than on live stems (Green and Edmisten 1974; Patriquin 1978; Casselman et al. 1981). The objectives of this research were to determine seasonal patterns in AR rates associated with standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems collected from both a mature, natural salt marsh and a transplanted salt marsh. Although results from diel experiments strongly implicated epiphytic cyanobacteria as the primary N_2-fixing microorganisms on standing dead Spartina stems (Currin and Paerl 1997), separate incubations of the epiphytic film and underlying stem were made to determine the physical location of the N_2-fixing activity. In addition, the effects of desiccation, ash content, and shoot part (stem versus leaf) on AR rates were examined. An estimate of the annual N input by the epiphytic community is made for both a mature, natural marsh and a young (<3 yr old), transplanted marsh. Materials and Methods Standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems were collected from adjacent natural and transplanted marshes in the Newport River Estuary, North Carolina. The created marsh was planted with Spartina alterniflora in June 1990 (Currin et al. 1996). Collections from the natural marsh were made from five sites in a transect extending from a short Spartina zone (one site), through tall Spartina (two sites), and ending in another short Spartina zone (two sites) in the upper intertidal. Spartina stems were also collected from five sites established in the transplanted marsh, which included tall-form and short-form Spartina zones. A survey of the marshes demonstrated that there is <0.3 m difference in tidal elevation among all of the collection sites (C. Currin unpublished data). Standing dead stems were defined as the stem portion of Spartina shoots that is yellow-brown to brown in color, may include old sheaths but not blades, and remains upright on the marsh surface. Stems were chosen either randomly, using quadrants and random numbers, or arbitrarily with no selection criteria other than that described above. On several occasions, newly senescent stems (yellow-brown color, leaves intact, height >40 cm) were distinguished from old dead stems (brown color, leaves absent, height <25 cm). For AR assays (described below), 4-cm stem sections were removed from the zone between 5 cm and 15 cm from the base of the stem. Sample collections in the adjacent natural marsh were made in April, June, and October 1991; August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May, and June 1993. Samples were collected from the transplanted marsh in April and October 1991; February, August, September, November, and December 1992; and January, March, May and June 1993. Additionally, results from submerged and aerial incubations from diel experiments run in March, July, and October 1992 and May 1993 (Currin and Paerl 1997) were included in estimates of annual N_2 fixation rates. The majority of incubations were done at midday (MD), defined as the period 1100–1500 hours. Incubations designated as evening (PM) were begun at or shortly after sunset (1730–2030 hours). Incubations designated as morning (AM) were begun near sunrise (0545–0800 hours). AR assays were used to estimate N_2 fixation rates (Hardy et al. 1968). All incubations were done in air, with the exception of submerged incubations in diel experiments (see Currin and Paerl 1997). After immersion in seawater (30–35%o) for 5 s, a 4-cm stem section was placed in a clean (HCl-soaked, distilled water rinsed) glass 38-ml serum bottle sealed with a rubber stopper. Seven ml of the headspace was withdrawn with a syringe, and replaced with 7.4 ml of CaC_2-generated acetylene. Bottles were incubated upright in a running water bath at ambient temperatures, when possible. Many of the incubations were done in the field, without access to running water, and so the bath water was changed periodically to minimize temperature changes. After a 2–3 h incubation, assays were terminated by injecting 9 ml distilled water, mixing, and withdrawing 9 ml of the headspace to an evacuated 9.6-ml serum bottle. The ethylene content of the headspace was determined by injecting 0.3-ml subsamples into a Shimadzu GC 8A gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a Poropak T column maintained at 80°C. N2 served as the carrier gas, and ethylene concentrations were determined by comparisons to standards prepared from pure ethylene (Matheson Gas Company). Upon termination of the AR assay, stems were removed from sample bottles and stem length and diameter recorded. Acetylene reduction rates are reported on a cm^2 basis, reflecting the stem surface area. In some instances, stem dry mass and organic matter content were obtained by drying for 48 h at 95°C, followed by ashing for 8 h at 500°C. The effect of desiccation on stem AR rates was examined on four occasions in September 1992 and once in December 1992. In the first experiment, stems from both marshes were collected during low and high tide periods of two consecutive tidal cycles, and incubated without any pretreatment (i.e., no seawater submergence). In subsequent experiments, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes ca. 60 min after slack low tide. Half of the stems from each marsh were immersed in seawater prior to AR assay (standard protocol), while the other half were placed in incubation bottles without the seawater immersion pretreatment. AR incubations were otherwise as described above. The potential locus of standing dead stem N2 fixation was determined in June 1991 and December 1992 by dissecting the epiphytic film away from the stem, and assaying both portions for AR. In June, 10 stems were collected from the natural marsh, and five stems were divided into epiphytic film and underlying stem portions. Dissection was done using a scalpel, and some fibrous Spartina material was retained in the epiphytic film. The remaining five stems were incubated intact. In December, 10 stems were collected from both natural and transplanted marshes and were treated as in June. Leaf blades attached to standing dead stems were assayed for AR on four occasions. The first or second leaf closest to the stem base was collected from the transplanted marsh in February, May, November, and December. Similar collections were made in the natural marsh in May and November. Leaves were immersed for 5 s in seawater prior to AR assay and treated as described above for stem incubations. The density of standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems was measured twice in the course of this study. On each occasion, 0.0625-m^2 quadrats were located randomly adjacent to the transects normally sampled for stem collections. The number of standing dead stems was measured in 10 replicate quadrats in each marsh. Statistical analysis was conducted with SAS software (SAS Institute Co., Cary North Carolina). One-way analysis of variance was used to determine significance of effects when class variables had three or more levels, and Tukey's test was used to determine the significance of differences between selected treatment means. Pairwise comparisons were done with t-tests. Data were log-transformed when necessary (fmax test), and significance was determined at p < 0.05. Results AR Rates in Natural and Transplanted Marshes There was no significant difference in AR rates (nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) between newly senescent and old standing stems in either marsh at any sampling time (t-test, p > 0.05). Therefore, data from senescent and old stems are combined in subsequent analyses. Leaves collected from standing dead stems in the natural and transplanted marshes had AR rates similar to stems, both on an areal (cm^2) and ash-free dry weight basis (p > 0.05). The only exception to this occurred in May 1993 when transplanted marsh stems had AR rates (4.26 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}) which were significantly higher than AR rates on leaves (1.31 nmol C2H4 cm^{-2} h^{-1}, t-test, p < 0.01). On an ash-free dry weight basis, however, standing dead stem and leaf AR rates were not significantly different at any sampling time. The average AR activity on standing dead Spartina alterniflora stems incubated at midday ranged from <1 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} in the natural marsh during November and December to 17 nmol cm^{-2} h^{-1} on stems collected from the transplanted marsh in July (Table 1; Fig. 1). Midday AR rates were significantly higher than morning or evening AR rates in December and May in the transplanted marsh and in March in the natural marsh. However, in the period July to October, midday AR incubations were equal to or significantly lower than morning or evening incubations (Fig. 1). On most sampling days, AR rates associated with standing dead stems from the natural marsh were equal to or lower than rates associated with stems from the transplanted marsh. The most distinct break in this pattern occurred in April 1991, when AR rates on stems from the natural marsh were significantly higher than those from the transplanted marsh (ANOVA, p < 0.05). This occurred on the first sampling date, after only one growing season, and was the only occasion when well-developed epiphytic films were not observed in the transplanted marsh. TABLE 1.
